Here we present the dynamic universal encoding tensorcore (DUET), a general-purpose photonic computing paradigm based on vectorized operand differential interferometric cells (VODICs). By exploiting inherent structural symmetry, this design provides a full-range linear encoding interface that directly accommodates signed operands. This approach eliminates the sign-based path splitting, nonlinear remapping, and auxiliary preprocessing typically required in conventional ONNs, thereby reducing latency and minimizing hardware and memory overhead. We further implement a hardware-aware training (HAT) strategy to alleviate the impact of on-chip non-idealities and ensure stable inference. DUET is experimentally validated across diverse architectures and application domains, ranging from image classification and medical segmentation to Transformer-based content generation, demonstrating competitive performance. By extending optical computing to universal, full-range operators across diverse model architectures, DUET provides a viable pathway toward general-purpose optical acceleration for contemporary AI workloads.
tldr: This paper presents a photonic computing primitive (DUET) for accelerating AI workloads, but does not address the user's research interests in quantum information thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Existing optical neural networks suffer from hardware overhead and limited support for arbitrary matrix operations needed for modern AI.
method: The authors design a dynamic universal encoding tensorcore (DUET) based on vectorized operand differential interferometric cells (VODICs) that provide full-range linear encoding without sign-based path splitting, and implement hardware-aware training to mitigate non-idealities.
result: DUET is experimentally validated across image classification, medical segmentation, and Transformer-based content generation, achieving competitive performance.
conclusion: DUET offers a pathway to general-purpose optical acceleration for AI, but the work is focused on classical photonic computing and does not involve quantum effects or the user's specific research areas.

title: Classical State Preparation For Variational Quantum Algorithms Via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Gino Kwun, Dhanvi Bharadwaj, Gokul Subramanian Ravi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) potentially offer a pathway to practical quantum advantage, but their optimization is heavily hindered by barren plateaus and numerous local minima. While classically simulable Clifford circuits can warm-start VQAs to accelerate convergence, existing heuristic-based initialization methods struggle to scale within vast combinatorial search spaces. To overcome this bottleneck, we propose CRiSP (a Clifford Reinforcement Learning agent for State Preparation), a framework that formulates discrete prefix selection as a sequential decision-making problem. CRiSP utilizes Neural-Guided Monte Carlo Tree Search, driven by a Transformer-based policy trained via self-play, to insert learned Clifford gates before fixed parameterized rotations. This enables the construction of high-quality initial states entirely through polynomial-time classical stabilizer simulation without altering the underlying circuit architecture. By integrating a curriculum learning strategy that progressively expands the search horizon, the agent efficiently scales to deep circuits. Evaluated on QAOA benchmarks of up to [MATH] qubits and [MATH] parameters, CRiSP outperforms state-of-the-art Clifford initialization methods by a mean of [MATH] (max [MATH]) in average energy accuracy and [MATH] (max [MATH]) in best-achieved energy accuracy. Assessments on VQE tasks further demonstrate the framework's robustness and generalizability.
tldr: CRiSP uses reinforcement learning to generate classical Clifford-based initial states for variational quantum algorithms, improving optimization by avoiding barren plateaus.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from optimization challenges like barren plateaus and local minima; classical warm-starting can help but existing heuristic methods do not scale.
method: The paper formulates Clifford gate prefix selection as a sequential decision problem, using Neural-Guided Monte Carlo Tree Search with a Transformer policy trained via self-play, plus curriculum learning to scale to deep circuits.
result: CRiSP outperforms state-of-the-art Clifford initialization methods on QAOA benchmarks up to 40 qubits, achieving up to 6x improvement in average energy accuracy and 8x in best energy accuracy.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates that reinforcement learning can effectively generate high-quality initial states for VQAs, with potential for broader application in quantum algorithm design.

title: Exact Solution Of Generalized Gauge-invariant Ising Chains With Multi-spin Interactions
authors: Stepan Shchurenkov Pavel Khrapov
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, exact solutions are obtained for a class of generalized gauge-invariant [MATH]-chain Ising models ([MATH]) with arbitrary multi-spin interactions that are invariant under the local [MATH] gauge group. On a strip lattice of finite length [MATH] and width [MATH] with periodic or free boundary conditions, an explicit expression for the partition function is derived using the transfer-matrix method. Two successive transformations are developed: elimination of gauge redundancy and reduction of the original model to an effective [MATH]-chain Ising model with all possible interactions between neighboring vertical layers. On the basis of the spectral decomposition of the [MATH] transfer matrix, general formulas are obtained for gauge-invariant correlation functions and Wilson loops of arbitrary width. For [MATH], explicit expressions are derived in terms of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. A detailed analysis of the behavior of the Wilson loop is performed, which allows us to identify regimes exhibiting area-law (confinement-like) and perimeter-law (deconfinement-like) dependence. For specific Hamiltonians, the string tension is computed and the corresponding phase diagrams are constructed. The results generalize and substantially extend the classical works on the gauge-invariant Ising model.
tldr: This paper solves a class of gauge-invariant Ising chains with multi-spin interactions exactly using transfer-matrix methods, analyzing Wilson loops and phase diagrams.
motivation: To extend classical results on gauge-invariant Ising models to include arbitrary multi-spin interactions and to study confinement-deconfinement transitions.
method: Transfer-matrix method with two successive transformations: elimination of gauge redundancy and reduction to an effective Ising chain, followed by spectral decomposition.
result: Exact expressions for partition functions, correlation functions, and Wilson loops; identification of area-law and perimeter-law regimes; computation of string tension and phase diagrams.
conclusion: The results generalize known gauge-invariant Ising models and provide a framework for studying confinement in lattice gauge theories with multi-spin interactions.

title: A General Quantum Speed Limit For Non-Hermitian Systems
authors: Zhanxi Wang, Xiaozhe Hao, X. X. Yi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum speed limit (QSL) refers to the maximum speed of a quantum system to evolve from an initial state to its orthogonal states. The bound on the QSL for Hermitian systems, for example the Mandelstam-Tamm (MT) and Margolus-Levitin (ML) as well as Sun-Zheng(SZ) bound, was studied respectively from the perspectives of average value and variance of the system Hamiltonian as well as the geometry of the system. While the compactness of the MT-type, ML-type and SZ-type bounds has been examined well for Hermitian systems, a compact QSL for non-Hermitian systems has not been well studied. In this work, based on the biorthogonal basis theory we derive two distinct and tighter bounds on the QSL for non-Hermitian systems, which correspond to the MT and ML bounds for Hermitian systems. We show that the shortest evolution time corresponding to the two bounds of the non-Hermitian system can be attained by certain initial states, showing the compactness and tightness of our bounds. These initial states dubbed fastest initial states(FIS) are different from that in Hermitian systems. A bound close to QSL for non-FIS is presented and comparison of our bound with others in literature is performed. To illustrate our results, we present a minimal non-Hermitian system to show QSL, and the condition for the shortest evolution time is derived analytically using the present theory.
tldr: This paper derives tighter quantum speed limits for non-Hermitian systems using biorthogonal basis theory.
motivation: Quantum speed limits for non-Hermitian systems were not well studied, and existing bounds lacked compactness.
method: The authors use biorthogonal basis theory to derive two distinct bounds analogous to the Mandelstam-Tamm and Margolus-Levitin bounds for Hermitian systems.
result: They obtain tighter bounds that are attainable by certain 'fastest initial states', and provide a minimal non-Hermitian system example.
conclusion: The work provides compact QSL bounds for non-Hermitian systems, with potential applications in open quantum systems and non-Hermitian physics.

title: Accelerating Ground State Search Of Spatial Photonic Ising Machines With Genetic-simulated Annealing Hybrid Algorithm
authors: Ze Zheng, Ruhui Ni, Jingyi Zhao, Xiaojian Hu, Wen Jiang, Yuegang Li, Hang Xu, Tailong Xiao, Guihua Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial photonic Ising machines (SPIMs) based on spatial light modulators (SLMs) have emerged as highly effective solvers for many tasks, including combinatorial optimization problems and spin-glass simulations. However, traditional SPIMs relying solely on the simulated annealing algorithm require a large number of measurement-feedback iterations to find a relatively optimal solution in complex energy landscapes, suffering from slow convergence and high time cost. Here, we propose an optical genetic-simulated annealing hybrid algorithm to accelerate the ground-state search of SPIMs. GA conducts a global coarse-grained search in the early iteration stage, while SA performs fine-grained local refinement in the late stage. Numerical simulations show that our method enables a higher solution quality of full-rank Max-Cut problems than pure GA or SA at different scales. We also experimentally demonstrate its superiority over conventional algorithms on a gauge-transformation time-division multiplexing SPIM for high-rank optimization problems under the same iteration budget. Our approach can be further developed with other advanced metaheuristic algorithms toward intelligent optical Ising computing systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid genetic-simulated annealing algorithm to accelerate ground-state search in spatial photonic Ising machines for combinatorial optimization.
motivation: Traditional SPIMs using simulated annealing converge slowly and require many iterations for complex energy landscapes.
method: The hybrid algorithm uses genetic algorithm for global coarse-grained search in early iterations and simulated annealing for fine-grained local refinement later.
result: Numerical simulations show higher solution quality for full-rank Max-Cut problems than pure GA or SA; experiments on a gauge-transformation time-division multiplexing SPIM demonstrate superiority under same iteration budget.
conclusion: The approach can be extended with other metaheuristic algorithms toward intelligent optical Ising computing systems.

title: Approaching Physical Limits Of Latent Dimensionality In Optical Computing
authors: Zhenyu Zhao, Zijun Qiu, Xuan Hu, Yao Zhou, Jinlong Xiang, Youlve Chen, Chaojun Xu, Yuchen Yin, Tao Lin, Yikai Su, Xuhan Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The physical implementation of artificial intelligence requires mapping computational processes onto the dynamic physical processes of the underlying computing platform. The photonic processors offer an intrinsically parallel and low energy framework for this mapping, however, a mismatch between the potential computing capability of a bounded optical domain and the human accessible manipulation range sets a hard integration density ceiling on existing architectures. Here, we address this challenge by investigating the integration density limits in photonic processors through exploring the fundamental physical limits on the latent dimensionality for maximum expressivity of a bounded optical domain. These physical limits potentially serve as universal metrics for evaluating optical computing capacity. To validate these, we design and realize ultracompact multimode photonic processors approaching these limits: a 2.2 um by 8 um processor achieves 86.7 % accuracy in experiment for iris flower classification, and a 20.6 um by 44.8 um processor reaches 92.9% accuracy in handwritten digit recognition. Finally, we scale this architecture to highly complex tasks by implementing a generative diffusion model for image synthesis. By grounding photonic processor design in the wave physics origin of latent dimensionality, our results supply the missing theoretical reference point for optical computing architecture.
tldr: This paper explores fundamental physical limits on latent dimensionality in optical computing and demonstrates ultracompact photonic processors for classification and image generation.
motivation: To address the mismatch between potential computing capability of bounded optical domains and human-accessible manipulation range, which limits integration density in photonic processors.
method: The authors derive physical limits on latent dimensionality for maximum expressivity of a bounded optical domain, then design and realize ultracompact multimode photonic processors approaching these limits, validated through iris flower classification and handwritten digit recognition, and scaled to a generative diffusion model.
result: A 2.2 μm × 8 μm processor achieves 86.7% accuracy on iris classification, and a 20.6 μm × 44.8 μm processor achieves 92.9% accuracy on handwritten digit recognition; the architecture is scaled to image synthesis via diffusion models.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical reference point for optical computing architecture by grounding design in wave physics, potentially enabling higher integration density and efficiency in photonic AI accelerators.

title: Safe ma-QAOA: Surrogate-Assisted And Fine-Tuning Enhanced Multi-Angle Qaoa With Parameter Distillation
authors: Youngseok Lee Hyunwoo Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multi-angle Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (ma-QAOA) extends the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) by assigning a larger number of independent variational parameters, thereby increasing expressivity and improving performance at low circuit depths. However, this larger parameterization makes training more difficult and requires repeated circuit evaluations for gradient-based optimization. In this work, we propose the Surrogate-Assisted and Fine-tuning Enhanced (SAFE) framework. SAFE first uses Low-Weight Pauli Propagation (LWPP) as a classical surrogate for pre-training ma-QAOA parameters before exact optimization. SAFE then applies parameter distillation, which removes angles that remain near zero after surrogate pre-training. Finally, SAFE performs exact fine-tuning by optimizing the remaining active parameters using the exact energy objective. We evaluate SAFE on instances of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, two-dimensional square-lattice spin glass, and Max-Cut. SAFE with distillation provides the strongest overall results relative to exact-only: (i) a 64.3 percent reduction in active parameter count and (ii) a 94.5 percent reduction in estimated QPU workload. Within the SAFE workflow, adding distillation further reduces the optimizer steps to the near-optimal regime by 44.4 percent relative to without distillation. These results provide evidence that SAFE ma-QAOA can accelerate convergence to high-quality solutions while reducing the required quantum resources for exact fine-tuning, offering a resource-efficient route toward expressive ma-QAOA on NISQ hardware.
tldr: The paper proposes a surrogate-assisted and fine-tuning framework (SAFE) to reduce quantum resources for training multi-angle QAOA on combinatorial optimization problems.
motivation: Multi-angle QAOA improves expressivity but requires many variational parameters and repeated circuit evaluations, making training difficult on NISQ hardware.
method: SAFE uses Low-Weight Pauli Propagation as a classical surrogate for pre-training, then applies parameter distillation to remove near-zero angles, followed by exact fine-tuning of remaining active parameters.
result: SAFE with distillation reduces active parameter count by 64.3% and estimated QPU workload by 94.5%, and reduces optimizer steps to near-optimal regime by 44.4% compared to without distillation.
conclusion: The framework offers a resource-efficient route to expressive ma-QAOA on NISQ devices, but the paper focuses on combinatorial optimization, not directly on the user's research interests.

title: Ancilla-Efficient Qsample Preparation For Reversible Markov Chains
authors: Nicholas Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing quantum samples (QSAMPLES), coherent encodings of stationary distributions of reversible Markov chains, is a fundamental primitive in quantum sampling, particularly for quantum simulated annealing. A central limitation of existing phase-estimation-based frameworks is the ancilla qubit overhead. In this work, we present a new end-to-end framework requiring only one ancilla qubit in the working register. The key technical ingredient is a selective phase compiler circuit using one ancilla qubit, built from a generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP)-based projector onto the 1-eigenspace of the qubitized Szegedy walk. Embedding these selective phase compilers into the fixed-point amplitude amplification (FPAA) procedure and iterating yields a quantum algorithm that, given an initial state, oracle access, lower bounds on the overlaps between adjacent states, and lower bounds on the phase gaps, outputs a QSAMPLE within any desired trace distance and thus total variation distance. The query complexity scales inversely with the square roots of both the minimum overlap and the minimum spectral gap of the Markov chains across the cooling schedule, up to polylogarithmic factors. We also perform simulations to verify how our qubit and query complexity evolve with the trace distance, and how this work compares to the previous framework. These results establish two improvements over the previous framework by Wocjan and Abeyesinghe. First, the working-register ancilla cost is reduced to one. Second, by inserting our GQSP-based selective phase compiler into the FPAA procedure, we improve the QSAMPLE transport overlap dependence from inverse minimum overlap to inverse square-root minimum overlap, relative to their Grover pi-over-three fixed-point method. Finally, as a direct application, we apply the quantum algorithm to prepare a Gibbs QSAMPLE and obtain a rigorous complexity analysis.
tldr: This paper presents an ancilla-efficient quantum algorithm for preparing quantum samples of reversible Markov chains using only one ancilla qubit and improved query complexity.
motivation: Existing phase-estimation-based frameworks for QSAMPLE preparation require many ancilla qubits, limiting near-term implementation. The goal is to reduce ancilla overhead and improve query complexity.
method: The authors construct a selective phase compiler using generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) with one ancilla qubit, embed it into fixed-point amplitude amplification (FPAA), and iterate to prepare QSAMPLEs.
result: The algorithm uses only one ancilla qubit, and its query complexity scales as inverse square root of minimum overlap and spectral gap, improving over previous work. Simulations verify performance.
conclusion: This work reduces ancilla cost and improves overlap dependence, making QSAMPLE preparation more practical for quantum simulated annealing and Gibbs state preparation.

title: Hyperedge Approximation For Stochastic Processes On Higher-order Networks
authors: Anzhi Sheng, Alex Mcavoy, Ye Tian, Silun Zhang, Angela Fontan, Joshua B. Plotkin
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphs are a standard framework for describing dynamical processes shaped by pairwise interactions among agents. But many systems involve interactions in groups of three or more agents. Here, we develop a method of "[MATH]-hyperedge approximation", a framework to analyze stochastic population processes on regular hypergraphs, in which each individual belongs to [MATH] groups of size [MATH]. The framework accommodates both higher-order interactions that determine payoffs and higher-order processes for updating states in response to payoffs. Applied to evolutionary game dynamics, the framework generalizes the classical pairwise result on benefits and costs, [MATH], that favors the spread of cooperation; and it provides critical benefit-to-cost ratios for nonlinear [MATH]-player public goods games that cannot be reduced to pairwise interactions. Applied to complex contagions, where inheritance of states occurs within hyperedges rather than along parent-offspring edges, the framework gives a closed-form result for the fixation probability, which shows how a complexity parameter governs the spread of rare types. Coupling the two processes produces a single stochastic model of payoff-biased complex contagion in structured populations. These results extend pair approximation from graphs to hypergraphs, accommodating multi-way interactions and inheritance structures with no pairwise analog.
tldr: This paper develops a hyperedge approximation method to analyze stochastic processes on regular hypergraphs, focusing on evolutionary game dynamics and complex contagions.
motivation: Many real-world systems involve group interactions beyond pairwise, but standard graph-based methods cannot capture higher-order effects. The authors aim to extend pair approximation to hypergraphs.
method: They introduce a hyperedge approximation framework for regular hypergraphs, where each node belongs to a fixed number of groups of a given size. The method generalizes pair approximation to account for multi-way interactions and inheritance structures.
result: The framework yields closed-form conditions for cooperation in evolutionary games (generalizing the classical benefit-to-cost ratio) and fixation probabilities for complex contagions, revealing a complexity parameter governing spread.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical tool for studying dynamics on higher-order networks, with implications for understanding cooperation and contagion in systems with group interactions.

title: Self-Orthogonal Twisted Generalized Reed-Solomon Codes And Their Application To Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Yanxin Chen, Yanli Wang, Tongjiang Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, two classes of twisted generalized Reed-Solomon (TGRS) codes with multi-twists are studied. Firstly, some sufficient and necessary conditions for these codes to be self-orthogonal and self-dual are established. Then several explicit constructions of self-orthogonal and self-dual codes are presented, from which quantum stabilizer codes are further derived. Finally, some corresponding examples are given, especially that some of these codes are MDS, AMDS or NMDS and that some of the resulting quantum stabilizer codes are optimal, achieving the quantum Singleton bound.
tldr: This paper constructs self-orthogonal and self-dual twisted generalized Reed-Solomon codes and derives quantum stabilizer codes from them, some of which are optimal MDS codes.
motivation: To expand the family of quantum stabilizer codes with good parameters by using twisted generalized Reed-Solomon codes, which offer more flexibility than classical Reed-Solomon codes.
method: The authors study two classes of TGRS codes with multi-twists, derive sufficient and necessary conditions for self-orthogonality and self-duality, and then construct quantum stabilizer codes via the CSS construction.
result: Several explicit self-orthogonal and self-dual TGRS codes are presented, and the resulting quantum stabilizer codes include MDS, AMDS, and NMDS codes, some achieving the quantum Singleton bound.
conclusion: The work provides new constructions of optimal quantum stabilizer codes, but the relevance to the user's interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid systems is indirect.

title: Abstract Theory Of Bogoliubov Linearizations With Application To Nonlinear Thermodynamic Formalism
authors: Jean-Bernard Bru, Walter de Siqueira Pedra, Artur Oscar Lopes
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bogoliubov's 1947 approximation, originally developed in the microscopic theory of superfluidity, laid the foundation for solving previously intractable quantum models and later became part of "quantum mathematics". Regarding mathematically rigorous results, one of its most advanced forms - the only one that handles quantum equilibrium states - was published in the Memoirs of the AMS in 2013. Building on key results from convex analysis, the present work significantly extends it to obtain a general mathematical theory that enables nonlinear variational problems on convex compact spaces to be fully studied via a linearization process, referred to here as the "Bogoliubov linearization". This problem is particularly timely, given the current development of quantum algorithms and computers, which are inherently linear machines. A deep connection with the optimal transport is also proven. As a paradigmatic example of application, the approach proposed here is applied to the nonlinear thermodynamic formalism - an emerging field that can have important impacts on various fields of mathematics, such as ergodic transport, the fractals and multifractal formalism, discrete-time linear dynamics, C*-algebras, etc. Notably, even in the case of finite alphabets the obtained results go beyond the scope of the existing literature in nonlinear thermodynamic formalism.
tldr: This paper develops a general mathematical theory for Bogoliubov linearizations to study nonlinear variational problems, with application to nonlinear thermodynamic formalism.
motivation: To extend Bogoliubov's approximation beyond its original context and provide a rigorous framework for nonlinear variational problems on convex compact spaces, motivated by the development of quantum algorithms and computers.
method: The authors build on convex analysis and previous rigorous results on Bogoliubov approximations to create a general linearization process, and prove a deep connection with optimal transport.
result: The theory enables full study of nonlinear variational problems via linearization, and is applied to nonlinear thermodynamic formalism, yielding results that go beyond existing literature even for finite alphabets.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational mathematical tool that could impact fields like ergodic transport, fractals, and C*-algebras, but its direct relevance to the user's specific research interests is limited.

title: Encrypted Neural Networks Without Overflows
authors: Philipp Kern, Lorenzo Rovida, Samuel Teuber, Edoardo Manino, Carsten Sinz, Alberto Leporati
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables private inference by evaluating neural networks on encrypted data. In this way, we can delegate the computation to a third party server without ever revealing the user's data. Currently, the CKKS scheme is the backbone of most efficient FHE implementations, but it only supports addition, multiplication, and array rotation operations, thus requiring all activation functions of the neural network to be approximated by polynomials within a certain interval, imposing strict design tolerances. In this paper, we demonstrate for the first time that this scheme is vulnerable to overflow attacks, i.e., seemingly benign inputs that can exceed such tolerances of the FHE circuit, thereby causing corrupt and unusable outputs. To avoid them, we propose a formal verification technique that computes certified bounds on the ranges of all neurons in the network. By construction, our method eliminates overflows and, in our experiments, removed observed overflows on all benchmarks, reducing failure rates from up to 47% to 0%. Moreover, our overflow-free solution is compatible with most CKKS-based frameworks, as it allows to simply substitute standard polynomials by polynomials with rigorously designed ranges.
tldr: This paper identifies overflow attacks in CKKS-based encrypted neural networks and proposes a formal verification technique to eliminate them.
motivation: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) for neural networks relies on polynomial approximations of activation functions, which can overflow with certain inputs, causing corrupt outputs. The authors aim to prevent such overflows.
method: The authors develop a formal verification technique that computes certified bounds on neuron ranges, ensuring that polynomial approximations stay within safe intervals.
result: The method eliminates overflows on all benchmarks, reducing failure rates from up to 47% to 0%.
conclusion: The overflow-free solution is compatible with most CKKS-based frameworks and allows substitution of standard polynomials with rigorously designed ones.

title: The Cognitive Kardashev Scale: Quantifying The Material Envelope Of Civilisational Computation
authors: Sachin Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much thinking can a civilisation do? Kardashev's (1964) typology ranks civilisations by total power: planetary (Type I, ~10^16 W), stellar (Type II, ~10^26 W), galactic (Type III). This paper builds an analogous Cognitive Kardashev Scale: how much sustained AI-grade computation each tier could support. Four ingredients enter the calculation: total power P (watts), the share f of it devoted to cognition, the efficiency [MATH] at which energy becomes compute (operations per joule), and the brain's own processing rate [MATH] as a reference unit. Anchoring on 2024-2026 hardware (El Capitan, NVIDIA Blackwell, Vera Rubin) gives [MATH] FLOP/J. Contemporary humanity sits at [MATH], three-quarters of the way to Type I. At Type I and [MATH], available compute is, within an order of magnitude, one personal AI's worth of cognition per human inhabitant; at Type II it is essentially incomprehensible. Three trajectories for frontier compute through 2035 are reported as conditional projections, not predictions. Whether the long-run binding constraint is energy or efficiency depends on engineering choices not yet made; the political economy of who has access may matter more than either.
tldr: The paper proposes a Cognitive Kardashev Scale to quantify the computational capacity of civilizations based on energy consumption, but it is a speculative thought experiment with no direct connection to the user's research interests.
motivation: To extend the Kardashev scale from energy to computation, estimating how much AI-grade computation different civilization types could support.
method: Combines total power, fraction devoted to cognition, energy efficiency of computation (FLOP/J), and a reference brain processing rate, anchored on current hardware benchmarks.
result: Contemporary humanity is three-quarters of the way to Type I; Type I yields one personal AI per human; Type II yields incomprehensible compute.
conclusion: The long-run constraint may be energy or efficiency depending on engineering choices, but political economy of access may be more important.

title: Strategic Coercion Within Alliances: The Greenland Sovereignty Game As An Ai Stress Test
authors: Peyton Williams Rommin Adl
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What happens when the strongest alliance member pressures a weaker member over territory and strategic control? We examine the Greenland sovereignty crisis as a stress test for LLM geopolitics, centered on the 2019-2026 U.S. push to acquire Greenland from the Kingdom of Denmark. The crisis nests two collective-action problems: Arctic strategic control and whether NATO can enforce alliance norms against the dominant member. We develop three games (asymmetric coercion; a NATO assurance game with a critical-mass tipping point; a triadic extensive-form game with social preferences) and test them with a multi-agent simulation in which eight frontier LLMs play six geopolitical roles (United States, Denmark, Greenland, NATO, Russia, Canada) across 3,604 completed games and 108,120 action observations. Using inverse game theory, we recover each model's structural utility parameters (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, eta) for material self-interest, reciprocity, inequality aversion, norm respect, and commitment consistency. Three findings stand out. First, all eight models become more escalatory under coercion framing (four-action escalation rises from 10.7% to 28.6%). Second, Chinese-origin models show systematically different power-weight profiles from Western-origin models when playing the U.S. role. Third, peaceful US acquisition emerges in only 1.9% of clean games and only 3 of 8 frontier models ever achieve it, most prominently DeepSeek V3.2, which executes a stable five-round playbook through the metropole. Prompts emphasizing jus cogens and self-determination reduce escalation back near baseline in the English-only confirmatory sample; multilingual contrasts are reported as exploratory sensitivity checks. We position this as a structural benchmark for LLM geopolitical behavior, complementing action-frequency benchmarks.
tldr: This paper uses LLM multi-agent simulations to model geopolitical coercion in the Greenland sovereignty crisis, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To test LLM geopolitical behavior and strategic decision-making under coercion, using the Greenland crisis as a case study.
method: Multi-agent simulation with eight frontier LLMs playing six geopolitical roles across three game-theoretic models, analyzed via inverse game theory.
result: All models become more escalatory under coercion; Chinese-origin models differ in power-weight profiles; peaceful acquisition is rare and achieved only by DeepSeek V3.2.
conclusion: The work proposes a structural benchmark for LLM geopolitical behavior, but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum computing, condensed matter, or machine learning.

title: Full-Scattering-Matrix Deterministic Phonon Boltzmann Transport Simulation
authors: Y. Sungtaek Ju
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solutions to the phonon Boltzmann transport equation under the relaxation-time approximation (RTA) are fundamentally limited in that they do not account for the off-diagonal elements of the scattering matrix, which encode intermode energy redistribution. We find that the phonon in-scattering matrix is globally incompressible, requiring nearly its full rank for any useful Frobenius accuracy. The incompressibility worsens as the Brillouin zone is refined. We show that, despite this difficulty, one can develop a computationally efficient 3D BTE solver incorporating the complete scattering matrix by leveraging our two structural discoveries: the non-equilibrium phonon distribution inhabits a remarkably low-dimensional subspace of mode space regardless of how many phonon modes exist, and the leading singular modes of the scattering operator align selectively with this transport-active subspace. Consequently, truncation incurs negligible transport error even under large norm error. The phonon streaming operator's mode-diagonal character further motivates a hybrid architecture that exploits these two properties. When applied to nanoscale structures emulating a fin field-effect transistor, our BTE solver quantifies a geometry-independent multiplicative correction to the temperature rise predicted under RTA. Our theoretical work and resulting BTE solver help enable rigorous study of phonon transport and systematic design of devices and structures in the ballistic and quasi-ballistic phonon transport regime.
tldr: This paper develops a computationally efficient 3D phonon Boltzmann transport equation solver that incorporates the full scattering matrix, revealing a low-dimensional transport-active subspace and a geometry-independent correction to RTA temperature predictions.
motivation: Standard relaxation-time approximation (RTA) neglects off-diagonal scattering matrix elements that capture intermode energy redistribution, limiting accuracy in ballistic/quasi-ballistic phonon transport. The authors aim to overcome this by developing a full-scattering-matrix solver.
method: The authors discover that the phonon in-scattering matrix is globally incompressible, but the non-equilibrium distribution lies in a low-dimensional subspace. They exploit this with a hybrid architecture combining streaming operator's mode-diagonal character and singular mode alignment.
result: The solver achieves high accuracy with negligible transport error despite large norm error from truncation. Applied to nanoscale finFET-like structures, it quantifies a geometry-independent multiplicative correction to RTA temperature rise.
conclusion: The work enables rigorous study of phonon transport in ballistic/quasi-ballistic regimes and systematic device design, but is focused on classical phonon transport rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Mid-infrared Single-pixel Imaging Via Two-photon Optical Encoding
authors: Huijie Ma, Kun Huang, Jianan Fang, Ziyu He, Yan Liang, Heping Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mid-infrared (MIR) imaging offers powerful capabilities for label-free chemical analysis, yet its practical deployment remains hindered by the high cost and cryogenic complexity of conventional cameras. Two-photon absorption (TPA) provides a promising route to room-temperature MIR detection, but existing TPA imagers based on raster scanning or array detectors are constrained by slow acquisition speed or limited detection sensitivity. Here we present a scanning-free MIR single-pixel imaging approach based on non-degenerate TPA in a silicon detector. The involved spatial encoding is realized by a near-infrared structured pump with a resolution of 7 [MATH]m, thus allowing high-fidelity MIR optical modulation through the phase-matching-free nonlinear interaction. Consequently, the spatially modulated TPA response is intrinsically integrated in the single-element photodetector, which favors computational reconstruction of the impinging MIR image by correlating measured intensities and predetermined patterns. Notably, the use of advanced algorithms of compressed sensing and deep learning facilitate image recovery under sub-Nyquist sampling with a compression ratio of 10\% and photon-starved illumination with an incident light flux of 0.5 pJ/pulse. Furthermore, a multispectral imaging over 2.5-3.8 [MATH]m is manifested for chemical discrimination of plastic films. The presented architecture would offer a broadband and sensitive alternative for MIR imaging in various fields ranging from biomedical diagnostics to material inspection.
tldr: This paper presents a mid-infrared single-pixel imaging technique using two-photon absorption in silicon, enabled by near-infrared structured illumination and computational reconstruction.
motivation: Mid-infrared imaging is useful for chemical analysis but limited by expensive cryogenic cameras; two-photon absorption offers room-temperature detection but existing methods are slow or insensitive.
method: Non-degenerate two-photon absorption in a silicon detector is combined with a near-infrared structured pump for spatial encoding, and images are reconstructed via compressed sensing and deep learning algorithms.
result: Achieved 7 μm resolution, sub-Nyquist sampling at 10% compression ratio, photon-starved detection at 0.5 pJ/pulse, and multispectral imaging over 2.5-3.8 μm for chemical discrimination.
conclusion: The approach provides a broadband, sensitive, and scanning-free alternative for mid-infrared imaging, with potential applications in biomedical diagnostics and material inspection.

title: Mid-infrared Nonlinear Pinhole Imaging
authors: Yanan Li, Kun Huang, Jianan Fang, Zhuohang Wei, Heping Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pinhole imaging is the most primitive and simplest lensless imaging paradigm, capable of transcending the physical limitations of conventional lens optics. This modality is particularly attractive for accessing a virtually infinite depth of focus or operating at extreme wavelengths. Here, we devise and implement a mid-infrared (MIR) pinhole imaging system at 3.07 [MATH]m based on nonlinear spatial filtering. Instead of using a physical aperture, the involved pinhole is optically formed by a near-infrared pump at 1.03 [MATH]m within a nonlinear crystal, which allows flexible and precise control over the effective aperture size to optimize imaging performance. Meanwhile, the MIR rays passing through the nonlinear pinhole are spectrally upconverted to facilitate sensitive imaging via a silicon camera. Consequently, the implemented upconversion pinhole imaging enables a large depth of field over 35 cm, beyond the reach of typical lens-based upconversion imagers. Furthermore, depth-resolving imaging across a large depth range is demonstrated in both the reflection and transmission modes based on time-of-flight and trigonometric techniques, respectively. The achieved capabilities -- featuring large operation depth, wide field of view, and flexible adaptability to various illumination conditions -- highlight the potential of the presented MIR imaging architecture for expansive scene detection and motion-aware applications in industrial inspection and night vision.
tldr: This paper presents a mid-infrared pinhole imaging system using nonlinear spatial filtering and upconversion detection for large depth-of-field imaging.
motivation: To overcome limitations of conventional lens-based imaging at mid-infrared wavelengths, such as limited depth of field and sensitivity issues.
method: A nonlinear crystal is used to create an optical pinhole via a near-infrared pump, and the MIR image is upconverted to near-infrared for detection with a silicon camera.
result: Demonstrated large depth of field over 35 cm and depth-resolving imaging in reflection and transmission modes.
conclusion: The technique enables flexible, high-performance MIR imaging for applications in industrial inspection and night vision.

title: On Global Attraction For A Particle Coupled To A Scalar Field
authors: Valeriy Imaykin
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the question of global attraction, in the energy norm, for finite energy solutions to classical particle coupled to a scalar wave field. The attraction could take place to either the set of the stationary solutions in the case of a confining potential or to the soliton manifold in the case of zero potential. By energy conservation argument we establish that in both cases there is no global attraction.
tldr: This paper proves that for a classical particle coupled to a scalar wave field, global attraction in the energy norm does not occur, contrary to some expectations.
motivation: To resolve whether finite-energy solutions of a particle-field system exhibit global attraction to stationary states or soliton manifolds.
method: Energy conservation argument applied to the coupled particle-wave field equations.
result: No global attraction to stationary solutions (confining potential) or soliton manifold (zero potential) in the energy norm.
conclusion: The system lacks global attraction, suggesting that long-time behavior is more complex; implications for nonlinear field theory.

title: Attosecond Shaping Of High-current Pulsed Electron Beams In A Home-built 37-keV Beamline
authors: Yuichi Tachibana, Marie Ouill\'e, Takuya Hosobata, Takashi Isoshima, Yoshiyuki Takizawa, Yutaka Yamagata, Yuya Morimoto
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultrashort electron pulses with a high average current provide a powerful means of enhancing time-resolved imaging and photon generation. In this study, we report the attosecond shaping of sub-relativistic electron beams using membranes in a newly developed apparatus that delivers a relatively high current (>2 electrons per pulse on a sample) with negligible space-charge effects. Optimizing the membrane arrangement minimizes the spread of electron-light delays to within a femtosecond over a wide range of incident angles. This enables the recording of attosecond streaking spectrograms, where net acceleration and deceleration, as well as monochromatization and energy broadening, are clearly observed. Through comparison with models, we estimate the durations of the bunched electrons to be 1.3 fs (FWHM) and 0.5 fs (RMS). Furthermore, we demonstrate the attosecond modulation of pulsed beams with a large energy spread originating from space charge effects. A modulation amplitude of 2 eV is shown to be sufficient to shape a beam with an initial spread of 15 eV (FWHM). These results represent a significant step toward the generation of an attosecond pulse containing one or more electrons.
tldr: This paper demonstrates attosecond shaping of sub-relativistic electron beams using membranes in a home-built beamline, achieving femtosecond-scale pulse durations and modulation of energy spread.
motivation: To enhance time-resolved imaging and photon generation by generating ultrashort electron pulses with high average current and minimal space-charge effects.
method: A 37-keV beamline with optimized membrane arrangements to minimize electron-light delay spread, enabling attosecond streaking spectrograms and comparison with models.
result: Achieved bunched electron durations of 1.3 fs (FWHM) and 0.5 fs (RMS), and demonstrated attosecond modulation of beams with large energy spread using 2 eV modulation amplitude.
conclusion: This work advances the generation of attosecond electron pulses containing one or more electrons, with implications for ultrafast imaging and photon sources.

title: SpinFlow: A Physics-Informed Spin Field Framework For Traffic Phase Inference And Transition Detection
authors: Haopeng Deng, Fucheng Zheng, Xinhai Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active traffic management (ATM) is frequently hindered by traditional macroscopic models and rigid empirical thresholds that fail to capture metastable phase precursors, resulting in delayed, reactive interventions. To address this, we propose SpinFlow, a physics-informed spin-field framework unifying Kerner's three-phase theory with statistical physics for continuous macroscopic traffic phase inference. Inspired by the Heisenberg model, SpinFlow parametrizes spatially varying phase weights via a latent spin vector and a competitive-equilibrium mapping, allowing synchronized flow to emerge naturally. A physics-regularized Expectation-Maximization algorithm inverts this latent structure from high-resolution trajectories, jointly optimizing the spin field while softly enforcing mass conservation and spatial smoothness. We introduce the Phase Equilibrium Degree (PED) to quantify structural alignment and topologically localize phase-transition points. Across four real-world trajectory datasets, SpinFlow achieves [MATH] up to 0.940, PED drops of 94.9-100%, and interpretable phase maps that outperform three heterogeneous baselines on forward accuracy, physics consistency, and bottleneck localization. SpinFlow pinpoints congestion nucleation without prior network topology, yielding a data-driven, physics-consistent trigger for ATM.
tldr: SpinFlow applies a spin-field framework inspired by the Heisenberg model to traffic phase inference, using physics-informed machine learning to detect congestion transitions.
motivation: Traditional traffic models fail to capture metastable phase precursors, leading to delayed interventions. The authors aim to unify Kerner's three-phase theory with statistical physics for better traffic management.
method: SpinFlow parametrizes phase weights via a latent spin vector and competitive-equilibrium mapping, using a physics-regularized Expectation-Maximization algorithm to invert the latent structure from trajectory data, enforcing mass conservation and spatial smoothness.
result: The method achieves high forward accuracy (up to 0.940), significant Phase Equilibrium Degree drops (94.9-100%), and interpretable phase maps, outperforming baselines in bottleneck localization without prior network topology.
conclusion: SpinFlow provides a data-driven, physics-consistent trigger for active traffic management, with potential for real-time applications and extension to other complex systems.

title: Inviscid Scaling In The Kuramoto-Sivashinsky Equation From Functional Renormalization Group And Direct Numerical Simulations
authors: Liubov Gosteva, Dipankar Roy, Nicol\'as Wschebor, L\'eonie Canet
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the one-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation features a scaling regime characterized by the dynamical exponent [MATH] at intermediate scales between the large-scale Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) scaling with [MATH] and the small-scale non-universal behavior. This scaling regime is intrinsic to the KS dynamics since it arises from the vanishing of the effective viscosity when evolving from its microscopic negative KS value, to its macroscopic effective positive KPZ value. This vanishing of the viscosity deeply imprints the behavior of correlations at intermediate scales, which exhibit a universal [MATH] scaling. This behavior pertains to the inviscid-Burgers universality class, which corresponds to the zero-viscosity fixed point of the KPZ equation. We evidence and characterize this so-far-overlooked scaling regime using both functional renormalization group and direct numerical simulations.
tldr: The paper studies scaling regimes in the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation using functional renormalization group and simulations, revealing an intermediate inviscid-Burgers scaling.
motivation: To understand the crossover from negative to positive effective viscosity in the KS equation and its impact on scaling behavior.
method: Functional renormalization group analysis combined with direct numerical simulations.
result: Discovery of an intermediate scaling regime with dynamical exponent z=1, belonging to the inviscid-Burgers universality class.
conclusion: The work identifies a previously overlooked universal scaling regime in the KS equation, relevant for pattern formation and turbulence.

title: Lowest Order Carleman Linearization For Steady State Fluid Flow Simulations
authors: Sauro Succi Luca Cappelli
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is shown that the lowest (second) order truncation of the Carleman linearization of the fluid equations (C2) recovers not only the initial transient of the time evolution but also its late stage, namely the steady-state solution. This asymptotic property is first proved analytically for the decaying logistic with external forcing and then shown to hold to a significant degree of accuracy also for the fairly more complex case of two-dimensional fluid flows at moderate Reynolds number. This time-asymptotic property opens interesting prospects for the simulation of steady-state solutions of the fluid equations on quantum computers.
tldr: This paper shows that second-order Carleman linearization can accurately capture steady-state solutions of fluid equations, with potential applications in quantum computing.
motivation: To explore whether low-order Carleman linearization, which is suitable for quantum computers, can reproduce steady-state fluid flows, not just transients.
method: Analytical proof for the logistic equation with forcing, and numerical simulations for 2D fluid flows at moderate Reynolds numbers using second-order Carleman linearization.
result: The second-order truncation recovers steady-state solutions accurately for both the logistic model and 2D fluid flows.
conclusion: This property opens prospects for simulating steady-state fluid dynamics on quantum computers using Carleman linearization.

title: Spatial Dealiasing Of Classical Geomagnetic Survey Data Through Use Of A Microfabricated Wearable Quantum Magnetometer
authors: Stirling Scholes, Alissa Forsythe, Courtney Dyer, Amy Gilligan, Karen Lythgoe, Jenny Jenkins, Marcin Mrozowski, Jack-Andrew Smith, Stuart Ingleby
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geomagnetic surveys provide insight into the subsurface for a range of applications, from fundamental understanding of geological processes, to mineral exploration and locating unexploded ordnance. A persistent challenge in performing such geomagnetic surveys is the joint problem of anthropogenic noise rejection and spatial aliasing, where the limited bandwidth (< 10 Hz) of traditional surveying instruments introduces artefacts into the surveyed field. Optically Pumped Magnetometers (OPMs) exploit quantum mechanical effects to achieve highly sensitive and stable magnetic field measurements at comparatively high bandwidths. Recent advances in manufacturing have enabled OPMs to be packaged in compact and lightweight systems (approx. 1kg), that are ideal for geomagnetic surveying. Here, we show how an OPM can directly contribute to the reduction of spatial aliasing in traditional PPM data. We carry both a PPM and OPM over a 20 km long transect across the Highland Boundary Fault (HBF) in Scotland. We leverage the continuous acquisition of the OPM sampling at 90 Hz, equivalent to every approx. 1 cm at walking pace (1 m/s) versus every approx. 200 m for our PPM (which had to be stationary for measurements) to reject magnetic noise and identify new small-scale (< 200 m) geological structures. Further, we discuss the logistical advantages of the hybrid survey in terms of portability, survey delivery, data density, and data quality.
tldr: This paper demonstrates the use of a wearable quantum magnetometer (OPM) to reduce spatial aliasing in classical geomagnetic surveys, revealing small-scale geological structures.
motivation: Traditional proton precession magnetometers (PPMs) suffer from low bandwidth and spatial aliasing, limiting resolution in geomagnetic surveys. The authors aim to overcome this by using a high-bandwidth OPM.
method: A hybrid survey was conducted carrying both a PPM and an OPM along a 20 km transect across the Highland Boundary Fault in Scotland. The OPM sampled at 90 Hz (≈1 cm spacing) while the PPM required stationary measurements (≈200 m spacing).
result: The OPM's continuous high-density data enabled rejection of anthropogenic noise and identification of new small-scale (<200 m) geological structures not visible in PPM data.
conclusion: Hybrid surveys combining OPMs with traditional magnetometers improve data quality and resolution for geomagnetic applications, with logistical advantages in portability and survey delivery.

title: Enhancing Broadband Second Harmonic Generation In A Thin Film Lithium Niobate Racetrack Resonator With Tunable-coupling
authors: Olivia Hefti, Jean-Etienne Tremblay, Andrea Volpini, Jannis Holzer, Alberto Della Torre, Homa Zarebidaki, Charles Ca\"er, Hamed Sattari, Camille-Sophie Br\`es, Davide Grassani
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Second harmonic generation in thin film periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) is constrained by an efficiency-bandwidth trade-off and fabrication-sensitive scaling. We demonstrate a racetrack resonator incorporating a short PPLN section and a tunable Mach-Zehnder interferometer coupler that enables in situ control of the coupling condition, compensating fabrication tolerances and stabilizing operation near critical coupling. The telecom pump is resonantly enhanced, while the near-infrared second harmonic is generated in single pass, eliminating dual-resonance requirements. The device achieves a 35 times efficiency enhancement over a non-resonant structure while maintaining a 7 nm bandwidth. This architecture provides a robust platform for broadband integrated frequency doubling.
tldr: A racetrack resonator with tunable coupling enhances second harmonic generation in thin film lithium niobate by 35x over non-resonant structures while maintaining 7 nm bandwidth.
motivation: Second harmonic generation in PPLN suffers from an efficiency-bandwidth trade-off and sensitivity to fabrication variations. The researchers aimed to overcome these limitations with a resonant cavity that allows in situ coupling control.
method: They designed a racetrack resonator integrating a short PPLN section and a tunable Mach-Zehnder interferometer coupler. The pump is resonantly enhanced while the second harmonic is generated in single pass, avoiding dual-resonance constraints.
result: The device achieved a 35-fold efficiency enhancement over a non-resonant structure with a 7 nm bandwidth, demonstrating robust broadband frequency doubling.
conclusion: This architecture provides a practical platform for integrated frequency doubling, compensating fabrication tolerances and enabling stable operation near critical coupling.

title: Resilience Characterization Of AI-Native Wireless Receivers Via Persistent Homology
authors: Emilio Calvanese Strinati Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-native wireless receivers based on deep learning exhibit remarkable performance under stationary channel conditions, yet their resilience to distributional shifts remains poorly characterized by conventional metrics such as bit error rate (BER). To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel real-time metric, the Topological Resilience Index (TRI), grounded in persistent homology and persistence exponents. TRI quantifies the structural stability of a neural network receiver's parameter space during online adaptation to non-stationary channels. Specifically, TRI captures resilience through three complementary dimensions: (i) validation-loss resilience measuring model-channel mismatch, grounded in the topological persistence of loss-landscape sublevel sets; (ii) channel impulse response (CIR) distribution shift, tracking geometric drift of CIR vectors from the calibration reference distribution; and (iii) channel manifold topology, quantified by the spectral gap of the Gaussian kernel matrix normalized by the Olivier-Ricci curvature norm. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that TRI is bounded, monotonic under performance degradation, and Lipschitz-stable with respect to perturbations in channel distributions measured in Wasserstein distance. Simulation results for an OFDM deep-learning receiver adapting across ten ITU-R inter-environment transitions at three shift rates demonstrate that TRI provides a consistent mean warning lead of more than one OFDM symbol over gradient-norm and validation-loss baselines, whereas the gradient-norm baseline achieves zero lead in every scenario. Furthermore, the proposed TRI-guided burst re-adaptation reduces post-shift BER by 80% relative to no adaptation within 200 OFDM symbols.
tldr: The paper proposes a topological resilience index (TRI) for AI-native wireless receivers to monitor distributional shifts, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or foundations.
motivation: Conventional metrics like BER fail to capture resilience of deep-learning receivers under non-stationary channels, motivating a new real-time metric.
method: TRI combines validation-loss resilience via persistent homology, CIR distribution shift tracking, and channel manifold topology using spectral gap and Olivier-Ricci curvature.
result: TRI provides earlier warnings than gradient-norm baselines and reduces post-shift BER by 80% with guided re-adaptation.
conclusion: Topological data analysis offers a promising tool for monitoring AI-native wireless systems, but the paper focuses on classical wireless communication, not quantum systems.

title: On Reed-Muller Subcodes, Grassmannian Partitions And Sum-free Functions
authors: Philipp Heering, Christian Kaspers, Vladislav Taranchuk
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A function [MATH] is called [MATH]th-order sum-free if the sum of its values over any [MATH]-dimensional affine subspace of [MATH] is non-zero. Carlet recently introduced this notion and constructed such functions for every [MATH]. We prove that, for [MATH] and [MATH], the existence of a (non-degenerate) [MATH]-valued [MATH]th-order sum-free function on [MATH] is equivalent to the existence of a codimension [MATH] linear subcode of the Reed-Muller code [MATH] with minimum distance [MATH]. In particular, this yields a new family of Reed-Muller subcodes that avoid all minimum weight codewords of [MATH], and thus have minimum distance [MATH] times that of [MATH]. We also derive new necessary conditions for the existence of [MATH]th-order sum-free functions and present the first nontrivial lower bound on [MATH]. Finally, we observe that [MATH]th-order sum-free functions lead to a partition of the Grassmannian of all [MATH]-dimensional (linear) subspaces of [MATH] into constant-dimension subspace codes. Under the assumption that functions exist that are [MATH]th-order sum-free for multiple values of [MATH], we obtain an improved partitioning result and a stronger upper bound on the chromatic number of the Grassmann graphs.
tldr: This paper studies sum-free functions over finite fields and their connection to Reed-Muller subcodes and Grassmannian partitions, with no direct link to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand the existence and properties of sum-free functions and their implications for coding theory and combinatorial designs.
method: The authors prove equivalences between sum-free functions and linear subcodes of Reed-Muller codes, derive necessary conditions and lower bounds, and use these to construct partitions of Grassmannians.
result: Existence of certain sum-free functions is equivalent to existence of Reed-Muller subcodes with high minimum distance; new necessary conditions and lower bounds are obtained; improved Grassmannian partitions and bounds on chromatic numbers are derived.
conclusion: The work advances combinatorial coding theory but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Performance Bounds For Rollout Policies In Stochastic Shortest Path Problems
authors: Bo Wahlberg Anders Hansson
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper concerns rollout and certainty-equivalent rollout policies for stochastic shortest path problems with absorbing terminal states. The main result provides a direct non-asymptotic performance certificate for a fixed rollout policy: the loss relative to the optimal value is controlled by the uniform accuracy of the value approximation and by the expected time for which the rollout closed loop remains away from the terminal state. Thus, in the undiscounted transient setting, the expected hitting time plays the role of a discount or finite-horizon parameter in more standard approximate dynamic programming bounds. This paper also gives a performance-difference identity showing that suboptimality is exactly accumulated through the transient occupation measure, and a deterministic sharpness example showing that the hitting-time factor is unavoidable. Finally, consequences under uniform hitting-time and Foster-Lyapunov drift conditions are given, and extend the argument to certainty-equivalent rollout by adding a separate local model-mismatch term.
tldr: This paper provides performance bounds for rollout policies in stochastic shortest path problems, focusing on undiscounted transient settings.
motivation: To derive non-asymptotic performance certificates for rollout policies in stochastic shortest path problems with absorbing terminal states.
method: The authors use a performance-difference identity and uniform accuracy of value approximation to bound suboptimality, with expected hitting time as a key parameter.
result: The loss relative to optimal value is controlled by the uniform accuracy of the value approximation and the expected time away from the terminal state; a sharpness example shows the hitting-time factor is unavoidable.
conclusion: The results extend to certainty-equivalent rollout under drift conditions, providing theoretical guarantees for approximate dynamic programming in transient settings.

title: Global Analysis Of The Kuramoto Flow
authors: Daniel Burns, Gregorio Malajovich, Charles Pugh, Indika Rajakapse, Steve Smale
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kuramoto's differential equation describes a synchronization process between several harmonic oscillators. It has been used to model biological phenomena such as the synchronization of heart cells, the circadian rhythm, or brain waves. It is also used in power system control. The simplest possible model assumes that all oscillators are identical and connected to each other with equal pairwise attraction. In this paper, we give a full geometric description of its global dynamics in terms of Morse theory and dynamical systems. Most of this description is stable in the sense that it is topologically preserved under small perturbations of the parameters.
tldr: This paper provides a global geometric analysis of the Kuramoto model's dynamics using Morse theory, but it does not address quantum systems, information thermodynamics, or quantum communication.
motivation: To understand the global dynamics of the Kuramoto model, which is widely used in biology and power systems, and to provide a stable geometric description.
method: The authors apply Morse theory and dynamical systems analysis to characterize the flow on the space of all-to-all coupled identical oscillators.
result: A full geometric description of the global dynamics is given, with most features stable under small parameter perturbations.
conclusion: The work advances mathematical understanding of synchronization but has no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Improved Torn Paper Coding Via Local Alignment
authors: Netanel Raviv Junsheng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the torn paper channel, a transmitted codeword is broken at random locations into fragments that arrive at the decoder in an unordered manner. A central theoretical challenge within this model is global alignment -- the task of determining each fragment's original position -- in order to faithfully reconstruct the entire codeword. Prior work by Shomorony and Vahid introduced an interleaved-pilot scheme that successfully achieved a vanishing error probability. However, their alignment strategy relies heavily on global statistics, requiring fragments to exceed a minimum length and effectively discarding many shorter ones as erasures, which results in rates significantly below capacity. To address this gap, we propose an improved coding scheme that achieves a provable rate increase through a novel approach we call . This approach identifies global alignment bits within each fragment using only local information, allowing the decoder to determine the positions of fragments that are shorter than those used in previous work. Consequently, the decoder can extract information from a much larger fraction of the channel output than in previous work, yielding significantly higher rates. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to torn paper coding with lost pieces (TPC-LP), a generalized model that accounts for length-dependent fragment deletion. For a class of TPC-LP channels that delete all fragments below a logarithmic length threshold while allowing arbitrary length-dependent deletion probabilities for longer fragments, we show that the proposed local alignment strategy achieves an arbitrarily small additive gap to capacity as the threshold increases.
tldr: This paper proposes an improved coding scheme for the torn paper channel using local alignment to increase achievable rates.
motivation: Prior work on torn paper coding relied on global alignment, which discarded short fragments and achieved rates below capacity. The authors aimed to improve rates by using local information to align fragments.
method: The authors introduce a local alignment strategy that identifies global alignment bits within each fragment using only local information, allowing shorter fragments to be used. They also extend the analysis to a generalized model with length-dependent fragment deletion.
result: The proposed scheme achieves a provable rate increase over prior work, and for a class of channels with logarithmic deletion threshold, it achieves an arbitrarily small additive gap to capacity.
conclusion: The work advances torn paper coding theory, but its relevance to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics is minimal.

title: Proximal Dca For Fr\'echet Regression On Riemannian Manifolds With Bounded Curvature
authors: C\'esar A. Uribe Yamin Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fr\'echet regression generalizes linear regression to metric-space-valued responses by defining fitted values as minimizers of weighted Fr\'echet functionals. Since these weights may have mixed signs, the resulting objective is a signed barycenter problem rather than a standard convex barycenter problem. On Riemannian manifolds, this is further complicated by the lack of global geodesic convexity and possible nonsmoothness of squared distances near cut loci. We study signed Fr\'echet regression on complete manifolds with two-sided bounded sectional curvature. By restricting optimization to a strongly convex normal ball containing the response support, we use local smoothness, Hessian comparison, and Jacobi-field estimates to formulate the problem as a locally controlled Riemannian proximal DC problem. This leads to FRIDA (Fr\'echet Regression via Riemannian Iterative DC Algorithm), an exact and inexact proximal DC algorithm for computing regression fits. We prove existence and interiority of minimizers under explicit signed-weight conditions, establish curvature-dependent strong convexity of the proximal subproblems, and show descent and convergence of the iterates to stationary points. We also derive sublinear complexity estimates and, under real-analyticity, obtain full-sequence convergence with KL-type local rates. These results provide a rigorous optimization framework for signed Fr\'echet regression on manifolds with bounded curvature.
tldr: This paper develops a proximal DC algorithm for signed Fréchet regression on Riemannian manifolds with bounded curvature, focusing on optimization theory rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Fréchet regression on manifolds with signed weights leads to nonconvex optimization problems; existing methods lack convergence guarantees for such settings.
method: The authors formulate the problem as a Riemannian proximal DC (Difference of Convex) problem, propose FRIDA algorithm (exact and inexact variants), and prove convergence using Hessian comparison and Jacobi-field estimates.
result: They prove existence of minimizers under signed-weight conditions, curvature-dependent strong convexity of subproblems, descent and convergence to stationary points, sublinear complexity, and under real-analyticity, full-sequence convergence with KL rates.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous optimization framework for signed Fréchet regression on manifolds, with potential applications in statistics and machine learning, but no direct connection to quantum computing or information thermodynamics.

title: Mode-Shape Expansion Using Physics-Constrained Gaussian Process Regression
authors: Farid Ghahari
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing full-field structural mode shapes from sparse sensor data. While Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) offers a robust non-parametric framework for spatial interpolation and uncertainty quantification, standard formulations often yield physically inconsistent mode-shape reconstructions under sparse sensing conditions. A Physics-Constrained Single-Output Gaussian Process (CONS-SOGP) framework is derived that utilizes independent modal kernels while coupling the optimization via a mass-orthogonality penalty. The paper presents derivations for the marginal likelihood, hyperparameter gradients, and penalty coupling. Numerical verification on a multi-degree-of-freedom structure demonstrates that the proposed method overcomes existing limitations in GP-based prediction, providing more accurate and reliable expanded mode shapes.
tldr: This paper develops a physics-constrained Gaussian process regression method for reconstructing structural mode shapes from sparse sensor data.
motivation: Standard Gaussian process regression often yields physically inconsistent mode-shape reconstructions when sensor data is sparse, motivating the need for a method that enforces physical constraints.
method: The authors propose a Physics-Constrained Single-Output Gaussian Process (CONS-SOGP) framework that uses independent modal kernels and couples optimization via a mass-orthogonality penalty.
result: Numerical verification on a multi-degree-of-freedom structure shows that the proposed method overcomes limitations of existing GP-based predictions, providing more accurate and reliable expanded mode shapes.
conclusion: The method improves mode-shape reconstruction accuracy and reliability, with potential applications in structural health monitoring and vibration analysis.

title: The Closure Of LCD-to-GI Reductions Via Generalized Inner Products
authors: Keita Ishizuka
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Permutation Equivalence Problem (PEP) for linear codes is a fundamental problem in coding theory and cryptography. A recent reduction shows that PEP for Linear Complementary Dual (LCD) codes reduces to Graph Isomorphism (GI) via orthogonal projectors, but is restricted to codes with trivial hull. We prove that this approach extends to bilinear forms [MATH], and that no other nondegenerate symmetric form yields a valid reduction. A code is reducible if and only if its hull dimension is at most [MATH] with an explicit condition on the hull vector; in characteristic [MATH], only LCD codes are reducible. This establishes the closure of the orthogonal projector method. We derive exact enumeration formulas via character sums over quadratic forms and provide a polynomial-time reduction algorithm.
tldr: This paper studies reductions from LCD code permutation equivalence to graph isomorphism via generalized inner products, focusing on coding theory and cryptography.
motivation: To extend the known reduction from LCD codes to GI beyond codes with trivial hull, and to characterize which bilinear forms yield valid reductions.
method: Uses algebraic methods including bilinear forms, character sums over quadratic forms, and analysis of hull dimensions.
result: Proves that the reduction works only for nondegenerate symmetric forms with specific conditions, and that only LCD codes are reducible in characteristic 2.
conclusion: Establishes closure of the orthogonal projector method and provides enumeration formulas and a polynomial-time reduction algorithm.

title: Fourier--Galerkin Methods For Subwavelength Resonances In 2d Acoustic Metamaterials
authors: Jinghao Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a Fourier--Galerkin framework for the analysis and computation of subwavelength resonances in two-dimensional scattering problems in finite domains. Starting from the boundary integral formulation, we project the operator onto Fourier modes and derive an explicit finite-dimensional effective matrix whose singularity characterizes the resonant frequencies. In the subwavelength regime, we obtain asymptotic expansions of this matrix in terms of [MATH] and the material contrast, identifying the leading-order operators and their kernel structure. This reduction transforms the resonance problem into a low-dimensional nonlinear eigenvalue problem, avoiding large-scale discretizations and global root-search procedures. The entries of the effective matrix are explicitly computable and admit fast evaluation using FFT-based quadrature. The resulting approach provides an efficient and robust computational framework for resonances in general smooth geometries.
tldr: A Fourier-Galerkin method is developed to efficiently compute subwavelength resonances in 2D acoustic metamaterials.
motivation: To overcome computational challenges in solving resonance problems for acoustic metamaterials, which typically require large-scale discretizations and global root-finding.
method: The boundary integral formulation is projected onto Fourier modes, yielding a low-dimensional nonlinear eigenvalue problem whose entries are computed via FFT-based quadrature.
result: Asymptotic expansions of the effective matrix in the subwavelength regime identify leading-order operators and kernel structure, enabling efficient resonance computation.
conclusion: The framework provides an efficient and robust computational tool for subwavelength resonances in general smooth geometries, with potential extensions to 3D and other wave phenomena.

title: Nonconforming Finite Element Approximation And Energy Lower Bound Estimation For The Gross--Pitaevskii Energy Functional
authors: Chen Zhang, Heyan Zhu, Wenbin Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ground state of Bose--Einstein condensates can be described as the minimizer of the Gross--Pitaevskii energy functional subject to a mass conservation constraint. In this paper, we study the corresponding discrete optimization problem in nonconforming finite element spaces and establish a priori error estimates for the discrete ground state energy, the discrete eigenvalue, and the discrete ground state. Specifically, we derive explicit convergence rates for the a priori error in the particular case of the [MATH] finite element. Furthermore, we proof that within the [MATH] finite element framework, the discrete ground state energy provides a lower bound estimation to the exact energy. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the theoretical analysis.
tldr: This paper develops nonconforming finite element methods for computing the ground state of Bose-Einstein condensates via the Gross-Pitaevskii energy functional, with a focus on lower bound energy estimation.
