conclusion: Provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for the Z-relation, but the results are confined to music theory and have no apparent application to the user's research interests.

title: Extremum Seeking With Exponential Convergence Via High-order Lie Bracket Approximations
authors: Sameh A. Eisa Victoria Grushkovskaya
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper focuses on the further development of the Lie bracket approximation approach for optimization and control via extremum seeking systems. Classical results in this area provide algorithms with exponential convergence rates for quadratic-like cost functions, and polynomial decay rates for cost functions of higher degrees. This paper proposes a novel design that ensures the motion of the extremum seeking system along directions associated with higher-order Lie brackets, thereby achieving exponential convergence for cost functions that are "flat-bottomed", i.e., polynomial-like but of degree greater than two and unlike literature assumptions, we do not require Hessian information or strictly non zero Hessian at the minimum. Numerical simulations are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed designs and their exponential convergence on fourth-, sixth-, and even eighth-degree cost functions. We include a comparison that shows our design outperforming a Newton-based method.
tldr: This paper proposes a novel extremum seeking control design using higher-order Lie bracket approximations to achieve exponential convergence for flat-bottomed cost functions.
motivation: Classical extremum seeking methods have limited convergence rates for cost functions of degree greater than two, and existing approaches require Hessian information. The authors aim to overcome these limitations.
method: The authors develop a control design that drives the system along directions associated with higher-order Lie brackets, enabling exponential convergence without Hessian knowledge.
result: The proposed method achieves exponential convergence on fourth-, sixth-, and eighth-degree cost functions, outperforming a Newton-based method in simulations.
conclusion: The work extends Lie bracket approximation theory to higher-order cases, offering a new tool for optimization and control of systems with flat-bottomed cost functions.

title: Delay-induced Dynamics In A Nonlinear Crime Interaction Model With Periodic Forcing
authors: Pablo Amster, Andr\'es Rivera, Sebasti\'an Pedersen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A nonlinear time-delay model is proposed to describe the interaction dynamics between criminal and non-criminal populations, combining social influence mechanisms, saturation effects represented by a Holling type II functional response, and time-dependent law-enforcement actions. The delay accounts for the latency between exposure to criminal behavior and behavioral response, introducing memory effects that naturally lead to a delay differential equations framework. Fundamental analytical properties, including positivity, global existence, and invariance of the feasible region, are established to ensure the mathematical consistency of the population interpretation. In the autonomous setting, explicit threshold conditions governing the stability of the criminal-free equilibrium and the emergence of coexistence states are derived, while the delay is shown to induce stability switches and oscillatory regimes through characteristic root crossings. In the non-autonomous case, topological degree arguments guaranty the existence of strictly positive periodic solutions, indicating that long-term dynamics depend primarily on the averaged law enforcement intensity measures rather than on short-term fluctuations. These results identify time delay as a key structural mechanism underlying recurrent patterns and complex temporal behavior in crime dynamics.
tldr: This paper models crime dynamics using delay differential equations with Holling type II functional response and periodic forcing, focusing on stability and periodic solutions.
motivation: To understand how time delay and law enforcement intensity affect crime patterns, particularly recurrent and oscillatory behavior.
method: A nonlinear time-delay model is proposed, analyzed for positivity, global existence, and invariance. Stability analysis via characteristic roots and topological degree arguments for periodic solutions.
result: Delay induces stability switches and oscillatory regimes; periodic solutions exist under averaged law enforcement intensity.
conclusion: Time delay is a key mechanism for recurrent crime patterns; future work could explore more complex social factors.

title: Inequalities On A Class Of Function Sets
authors: Gangsong Leng
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a functional extension of an exponential inequality originally proposed by Bin Zhao and proved by Xiaosheng Mou. The main result asserts that if [MATH] and [MATH], then \[ \sum_{k=1}^n \phi(k\alpha_k)\geq 0 \] for every odd function [MATH] that is increasing and convex on [MATH]. The proof is based on a truncated-sum comparison and the stop-loss characterization of the increasing convex order. As consequences, we recover the original exponential inequality and obtain polynomial and integral variants.
tldr: The paper proves a functional inequality involving odd convex functions and a sum of weighted terms, extending an exponential inequality.
motivation: To generalize a known exponential inequality to a broader class of functions and provide new variants.
method: Uses truncated-sum comparison and stop-loss characterization of increasing convex order.
result: Establishes that for certain sequences and an odd increasing convex function, the sum of function values is nonnegative.
conclusion: The result recovers the original inequality and yields polynomial and integral forms, but has no apparent connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: High-order Conservative Discontinuous Galerkin Methods Via Implicit Penalization For The Generalized Korteweg-de Vries Equation And The Hirota-Satsuma KdV System
authors: M. Shan Tariq, Yanlai Chen, Bo Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop new conservative discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods for nonlinear wave problems, focusing on the generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) equation and the coupled Hirota-Satsuma KdV (HS-KdV) system. The proposed methods preserve mass through the single-valued structure of numerical traces, while energy and Hamiltonian conservation are enforced by implicitly determining penalty parameters in the numerical traces through auxiliary conservation constraints. In our previous work [11], we developed a conservative DG method for the gKdV equation; however, that formulation involves the time derivative of the jump of the approximate solution, which complicates extensions beyond second-order temporal accuracy. Our new formulation overcomes this limitation by introducing a redesigned trace configuration that eliminates the derivative-of-jump term. This novel enhancement seamlessly paves the way for higher-order time discretizations and requires solving fewer nonlinear systems per time step than the previous approach. For the coupled HS-KdV system, we present the first conservative DG method that preserves all three invariants of the exact solution. Numerical results demonstrate the accuracy and expected convergence behavior of the proposed methods, as well as long-time stability and strong conservation properties for both the gKdV equation and HS-KdV system.
tldr: This paper develops high-order conservative discontinuous Galerkin methods for the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation and the Hirota-Satsuma KdV system, focusing on numerical conservation of mass, energy, and Hamiltonian.
motivation: To overcome limitations of previous conservative DG methods that involved time derivatives of jumps, which hindered higher-order temporal accuracy, and to extend conservation properties to coupled KdV systems.
method: Implicit penalization is used to determine penalty parameters in numerical traces via auxiliary conservation constraints, eliminating derivative-of-jump terms and enabling higher-order time discretizations.
result: The new methods preserve mass, energy, and Hamiltonian for both gKdV and HS-KdV systems, demonstrate expected convergence rates, and show long-time stability.
conclusion: The proposed DG methods provide a robust framework for simulating nonlinear wave equations with strong conservation properties, and can be extended to other conservative systems.

title: On Apn Exponents And The Differential And Boomerang Properties Of Binomials In Characteristic 3
authors: Namhun Koo, Soonhak Kwon, Minwoo Ko, Byunguk Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies on binomials of the form [MATH] over [MATH] have shown that these functions can exhibit very low boomerang uniformity. In this paper, we focus on the specific behavior of such binomials in characteristic [MATH], where instances of extremely low boomerang uniformity-namely [MATH] or [MATH]-seem to arise more frequently than in other characteristics. First, we provide a systematic analysis of Almost Perfect Nonlinear (APN) power functions in characteristic [MATH]. We present an explicit parametrization of APN exponents arising from the construction of Zha and Wang and demonstrate through numerical results for [MATH] that this generalized framework accounts for several previously known and sporadic APN instances. Building on this classification, we identify and rigorously prove two classes of binomials [MATH] that are locally-PN and possess the minimum possible boomerang uniformity of [MATH]. These classes involve exponents derived from the aforementioned APN construction and the differentially 4-uniform exponent [MATH]. Furthermore, we analyze the binomial [MATH] with [MATH], proving that it is locally-APN with boomerang uniformity [MATH] when [MATH] is odd, and completely determine its boomerang spectrum through the evaluation of character sums. Our results clarify and extend existing studies on the cryptographic properties of binomials, providing a systematic characterization of several classes of binomials with very low boomerang uniformity in characteristic [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies APN exponents and boomerang uniformity of binomials in characteristic 3, focusing on cryptographic properties rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To systematically analyze and classify binomials with low boomerang uniformity in characteristic 3, extending previous results on APN functions.
method: The authors provide a parametrization of APN exponents from Zha-Wang construction, prove classes of binomials with minimum boomerang uniformity, and evaluate character sums to determine boomerang spectra.
result: Two classes of binomials are proven to be locally-PN with boomerang uniformity 2, and another binomial is shown to be locally-APN with boomerang uniformity 4 for odd n, with full boomerang spectrum determined.
conclusion: The results clarify and extend the understanding of binomials with very low boomerang uniformity in characteristic 3, but the work is purely in cryptography and finite fields, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Miso Downlink With Fluid Antenna Multiple Access
authors: Anastasios Papazafeiropoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluid antenna multiple access (FAMA) enables each user to rapidly switch among several closely spaced ports and select the strongest received signal. Although this mechanism offers micro-scale spatial diversity, its behavior in multiuser downlink systems with spatial correlation and linear precoding is not well understood. This paper develops a unified analytical framework for the multiple-input single-output (MISO) downlink with FAMA users served via maximum ratio transmission (MRT) or zero-forcing (ZF). We show that the per-port signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) follows a Beta-prime distribution with parameters \((M_{},L)\), where \(M_{}=M\) under MRT and \(M_{}=M-U+1\) under ZF, and derive closed-form finite-sum cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) for both cases. We further provide the first analytical characterization of cross-port SIR correlation. {Furthermore, we derive rigorous outage probability bounds that tightly bracket the exact performance and become exact in the limiting cases of fully correlated and independent ports.} Asymptotic analyses reveal the fundamental diversity orders and tail behavior for each precoder. Numerical results confirm the accuracy of the SIR distributions, correlation model, and outage bounds, and show that MRT achieves weaker port correlation and larger selection gains than ZF when the base station (BS) has ample spatial degrees of freedom. The framework offers explicit guidelines for port configuration and precoder selection in practical FAMA systems.
tldr: This paper analyzes the performance of fluid antenna multiple access (FAMA) in MISO downlink systems with linear precoding, deriving SIR distributions and outage bounds.
motivation: The behavior of FAMA in multiuser downlink systems with spatial correlation and linear precoding was not well understood, motivating a unified analytical framework.
method: The authors develop a unified analytical framework for MISO downlink with FAMA users using MRT or ZF precoding, deriving closed-form CDFs for per-port SIR and cross-port SIR correlation, and providing outage probability bounds.
result: Key findings include that per-port SIR follows a Beta-prime distribution, MRT achieves weaker port correlation and larger selection gains than ZF when the BS has ample spatial degrees of freedom.
conclusion: The framework offers guidelines for port configuration and precoder selection in practical FAMA systems.

title: High-order, Long-time Stable And Parallel Decoupled GBDF$k$ Sav Ensemble Schemes For The Navier--Stokes--Darcy Flow With Random Hydraulic Conductivity Tensors
authors: Wei-Wei Han, Fukeng Huang, Changxin Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and analyze high-order ensemble schemes for the unsteady Navier--Stokes--Darcy system with uncertain initial conditions, forcing terms, hydraulic conductivity tensors, and Lions-Beavers-Joseph-Saffman interface conditions. The proposed schemes which are called GSAV-GBDF[MATH]-Ensemble schemes integrate a partitioned decoupling strategy, the generalized scalar auxiliary variable (GSAV) approach, and generalized BDF[MATH] discretizations. This framework achieves high-order temporal accuracy and long-time stability, permits explicit treatment of the nonlinear term, and facilitates an efficient ensemble implementation for multiple parameter realizations by sharing a single, unified coefficient matrix at each time step. Moreover, the numerical solutions are shown to satisfy uniform-in-time bounds without time-step restrictions. Owing to the ensemble formulation, the resulting linear systems share common coefficient matrices, which significantly improves computational efficiency. We further establish optimal-order error estimates for the proposed high-order schemes. Numerical results are included to confirm the theoretical analysis and to illustrate the accuracy, stability, and efficiency of the proposed methods.
tldr: This paper develops high-order ensemble schemes for the Navier-Stokes-Darcy system with random parameters, focusing on computational efficiency and stability.
motivation: To efficiently solve the unsteady Navier-Stokes-Darcy system with uncertain inputs, which is important for applications like subsurface flow and surface water coupling.
method: Combines generalized scalar auxiliary variable (GSAV) approach, generalized BDF discretizations, and a partitioned decoupling strategy to create ensemble schemes that share a common coefficient matrix across realizations.
result: Achieves high-order temporal accuracy, long-time stability without time-step restrictions, and significant computational efficiency through shared linear systems; optimal error estimates are proven.
conclusion: The proposed GSAV-GBDF-Ensemble schemes are accurate, stable, and efficient for simulating Navier-Stokes-Darcy flow with randomness, with potential for extension to other multiphysics problems.

title: Geometric Properties Of The Lebesgue Function
authors: Leokadia Bia{\l}as-Cie\.z, Stefano de Marchi, Mateusz Suder
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a collection of observations concerning the peculiar behavior of the Lebesgue function in the setting of the interval [MATH] and the square [MATH]. We provide numerical results and formulate several open problems related to the geometry of the Lebesgue function.
tldr: This paper studies geometric properties of the Lebesgue function on intervals and squares, with no connection to quantum computing, condensed matter, or machine learning.
motivation: To understand the peculiar behavior of the Lebesgue function in one and two dimensions.
method: Numerical experiments and theoretical observations.
result: Collection of observations and open problems about the geometry of the Lebesgue function.
conclusion: The work is purely mathematical and does not relate to the user's research interests.

title: Selective Ambulance Dispatch Under Contextual Travel-Time Uncertainty
authors: Zikun Lin, Daniel Zhuoyu Long, Viet Anh Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ambulance response is time-critical in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), where dispatchers must balance timely arrivals with limited fleet capacity. Static territories and deterministic travel-time estimates are vulnerable to dynamic congestion, while always-dual dispatch adds redundancy but consumes fleet capacity. We propose IDEAL (Intelligent Dual dispatch of Emergency AmbuLances), a selective dual-dispatch framework that sends a second ambulance only when the optimistic gap between primary and secondary paths exceeds a threshold. IDEAL learns context-specific edge travel times from trip-level dispatch records, including unobserved routes, using a weakly supervised bilevel representation network. We train the nonsmooth model with mini-batch conservative gradients and prove an asymptotic convergence guarantee. IDEAL models uncertainty via Burg-divergence perturbations to a shared metric in the learned representation space, thereby inducing correlated changes in edge travel times and learning context-specific radii from historical underprediction errors. For real-time decisions, IDEAL casts optimistic-gap computation as a difference-of-convex program and derives an efficient oracle with complexity guarantees. In collaboration with the Hong Kong Fire Services Department, we evaluate IDEAL using historical OHCA records and real-time adaptive simulations. The results achieve a stronger response-time/resource trade-off relative to all region-based and Google-based baselines.
tldr: This paper proposes a machine learning framework for selective dual dispatch of ambulances under uncertain travel times, focusing on operational efficiency in emergency medical services.
motivation: To improve ambulance response times for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest by balancing timely arrivals with limited fleet capacity, addressing limitations of static territories and deterministic travel-time estimates.
method: IDEAL uses a weakly supervised bilevel representation network to learn context-specific travel times from dispatch records, models uncertainty via Burg-divergence perturbations, and computes optimistic gaps via difference-of-convex programming.
result: The framework achieves a stronger response-time/resource trade-off compared to region-based and Google-based baselines in historical OHCA records and real-time adaptive simulations.
conclusion: The selective dual-dispatch approach can improve emergency response efficiency, with potential for integration into real-world dispatch systems.

title: Key Challenges And Bridges Among Convergence Analysis Techniques For Polytopal Methods
authors: Louren\c{c}o Beir\~ao Da Veiga, Daniele Antonio Di Pietro, J\'er\^ome Droniou
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polytopal methods provide a flexible framework for the numerical approximation of partial differential equations on general meshes. Their convergence analysis raises specific challenges due to their inherently non-conforming nature and, in many cases, the fully discrete nature of their solution. Two main techniques are considered: the virtual-function approach, used, e.g., in the context of Virtual Element Methods, and the fully discrete approach, which underlies, e.g., the Discrete de Rham method. We introduce here a novel framework based on the notion of conforming liftings, namely bounded and consistent mappings from the discrete space into the continuous space. This approach bridges the virtual and fully discrete viewpoints, clarifies the role of norm equivalence for virtual functions, and leads to a decomposition of the consistency error usable for polytopal methods. The three approaches are demonstrated on a model problem, which provides the opportunity to discuss relevant technical points. Bridges with the convergence properties of discrete differential complexes are also built.
tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for convergence analysis of polytopal methods in numerical PDEs, bridging virtual-element and fully discrete approaches.
motivation: To address the challenges in convergence analysis of polytopal methods due to their non-conforming nature and fully discrete solutions.
method: Introduces a novel framework based on conforming liftings, which are bounded and consistent mappings from discrete to continuous spaces, to unify virtual-function and fully discrete viewpoints.
result: The framework clarifies norm equivalence for virtual functions and decomposes consistency error, demonstrating the three approaches on a model problem.
conclusion: Provides bridges between convergence techniques and discrete differential complexes, offering a systematic tool for analyzing polytopal methods.

title: A Stochastic Implicit Proximal Point Algorithm For Solving Linearly Constrained Stochastic Minimax Problems
authors: Kehan Zhu, Jiani Wang, Yu-Hong Dai
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to solving large-scale minimax problems with nonsmooth regularizers. We propose a stochastic implicit proximal point algorithm with variance reduction techniques where stochastic oracles are selected in two cases -- with or without replacement. The semismooth Newton methods with Armijo line search is used to solve the implicit proximal point update subproblem in each iteration. The algorithm efficiently handles the strongly-convex-strongly-concave objective function with nonsmooth regularizers and coupling linear equations, which is proved to exhibit global q-linear convergence of the iterations to the saddle point and global r-linearly convergence of the multipliers to the multiplier set in expectation. Numerical experiments on machine learning problems demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both computational efficiency and selection of the step sizes.
tldr: This paper proposes a stochastic implicit proximal point algorithm for solving linearly constrained stochastic minimax problems with nonsmooth regularizers, demonstrating global linear convergence and numerical superiority on machine learning tasks.
motivation: Large-scale minimax problems with nonsmooth regularizers and linear constraints are challenging; existing algorithms often suffer from poor step size selection or slow convergence.
method: The algorithm combines stochastic implicit proximal point updates with variance reduction, using semismooth Newton methods with Armijo line search to solve the subproblem. Stochastic oracles are selected with or without replacement.
result: The method achieves global q-linear convergence of iterations to the saddle point and global r-linear convergence of multipliers in expectation. Numerical experiments show improved computational efficiency and step size robustness over state-of-the-art algorithms.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm offers a theoretically grounded and practically efficient solution for a class of minimax problems, with potential applications in machine learning and optimization.

title: Ra-dca: A Randomized Active-Set Dca For Directional Stationarity In Max-Structured Dc Programs
authors: Yi-Shuai Niu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study nonsmooth difference-of-convex programs whose subtracted convex term is a finite maximum of smooth convex functions. In this setting, standard DCA iterations may converge to critical points that are not directionally stationary, whereas exact active-vertex screening can be expensive when active sets are large or combinatorial. We propose RA-DCA, a vertex-first randomized active-set DCA that projects active gradients onto sampled directions, checks a sampled vertex residual, and uses a small linear program only as a low-residual convex-combination fallback. The method preserves the descent structure of DCA and reduces the randomized screening layer to matrix multiplications. Under the stated regularity, numerical active-set consistency, and random-embedding assumptions, every accumulation point generated by the safeguarded method is directionally stationary with probability one. MATLAB experiments first test the theorem on degenerate max-affine, max-quadratic, and sparse support-function models, where the safeguard avoids nonstationary critical points and closely tracks a full active-vertex scan. Block top-k tests then show that the same screening idea remains useful when exact aggregate enumeration is combinatorial. Trimmed-regression, complementarity, and QUBO diagnostics separate cases where active-set selection helps from cases dominated by multistart search, the DC split, or other problem-specific features.
tldr: This paper proposes a randomized active-set DCA for solving max-structured difference-of-convex programs, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Standard DCA may converge to non-directionally stationary points, and exact active-set screening is expensive.
method: RA-DCA uses vertex-first randomized active-set screening with gradient projections and a small LP fallback.
result: Under regularity assumptions, every accumulation point is directionally stationary with probability one; numerical tests on degenerate models and block top-k problems validate the method.
conclusion: The method offers a practical way to achieve directional stationarity in max-structured DC programs, but its relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is absent.

title: Non-colliding Billiards In The Plane
authors: Alexander Shamov Itai Benjamini
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an open problem about non-colliding freely moving hard disks in the Euclidean plane, together with related positive and negative partial results. The positive deterministic result gives a bounded, injective, non-colliding velocity assignment for the integer lattice. The negative result shows that no bounded continuous vector field on the whole plane can serve as a universal assignment satisfying the same separation inequality for all pairs of points at distance greater than one.
tldr: This paper studies non-colliding billiards (hard disks) in the plane, presenting an open problem and partial results on velocity assignments.
motivation: To understand whether there exists a continuous bounded vector field that prevents collisions among freely moving hard disks in the plane.
method: Mathematical analysis and construction of explicit velocity assignments for integer lattice points, and proof of impossibility for a universal continuous bounded vector field.
result: A bounded injective non-colliding velocity assignment exists for the integer lattice, but no bounded continuous vector field on the whole plane can serve as a universal assignment satisfying a separation inequality.
conclusion: The problem remains open for general configurations; the results highlight constraints on continuous velocity fields for collision avoidance.

title: Simulation Strategies For An Efficient Local Search To Solve Stochastic Scheduling Problems
authors: Philip de Bruin, Bram Elderhorst, Marjan van Den Akker, Han Hoogeveen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In scheduling problems, deterministic task durations are often assumed. This usually does not capture reality and may lead to schedules that are not robust to (small) changes to these task lengths. The use of stochastic task durations therefore seems preferable. Including these in local search, which is the way to find good solutions for difficult scheduling problems, is not straightforward, though. The objective value becomes stochastic then too, and computing the expected value is often not possible. One way out of this it to approximate this value by using simulation. This is quite easy to implement in a local search algorithm, but it may require many simulations each iteration to get a reliable estimate. Hence such an approach comes with a performance penalty. In this paper, we study techniques to limit the number of simulations. Besides comparing known techniques, we propose our own method for this, which is based on [MATH]-tests. We evaluate these techniques on the Stochastic Parallel Machine Scheduling Problem and the Stochastic Electric Vehicle Scheduling Problem. In these case studies, we show the effectiveness of using such methods to reduce runtime while retaining solution quality. Our method using [MATH]-tests turns out to be most effective in both problems.
tldr: This paper studies simulation-based local search methods for stochastic scheduling problems, focusing on reducing simulation runs using statistical tests.
motivation: Stochastic task durations in scheduling are realistic but make objective evaluation difficult; simulation is used but computationally expensive.
method: The authors compare known techniques and propose a new method based on statistical tests to limit the number of simulations in local search.
result: The proposed method using statistical tests is most effective in reducing runtime while maintaining solution quality for two stochastic scheduling problems.
conclusion: The work provides efficient simulation strategies for stochastic scheduling, with potential applications in other combinatorial optimization problems.

title: The Misattribution Gap: When Memory Poisoning Looks Like Model Failure In Agentic Ai Systems
authors: Tanzim Ahad, Ismail Hossain, Md Jahangir Alam, Sai Puppala, Syed Bahauddin Alam, Sajedul Talukder
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent AI pipelines typically assume that agent misconduct originates from model misalignment. We identify a structural failure in this assumption, the , where memory-layer attacks produce behaviors indistinguishable from model failure, causing defenders to apply the wrong remediation. We formalize (SND) as a third path to agent misconduct, distinct from emergent misalignment and collusion. In SND, a policy-formatted document enters a shared vector store through normal uploads and later reappears as trusted system context after provenance is lost through a Trust Laundering Chain. Across 64 documented failures, attribution systems consistently blamed the model. Four safety classifiers, including one trained on memory poisoning, produced zero detections across 510 checkpoints. In 59 of 65 valid cases, agents explicitly cited the injected document as normative authority before complying. The attack requires no trigger, model access, or repeated interaction, achieves full effect within five sessions, and persists indefinitely. We introduce Counterfactual Composition Testing, which identifies the causal entry with 87.5% accuracy and zero false positives, while a forensics baseline fails across all 25 scenarios. We further prove the Retrieval-Coverage Dilemma, showing that stronger evasion inherently weakens the attack, limiting adaptive bypass strategies. Finally, we propose Memory-Persistent Information-Flow Control, which blocks 97% of attacks at the cross-session boundary where prior defenses fail. We release the SND Corpus, the first adversarial memory benchmark with temporal persistence and multi-agent composition across financial and Health Care domains.
tldr: This paper identifies a new class of memory-layer attacks in multi-agent AI systems that mimic model failure, and proposes detection and mitigation methods.
motivation: Current multi-agent AI systems assume agent misconduct stems from model misalignment, but memory poisoning attacks can produce indistinguishable behaviors, leading to incorrect remediation.
method: The authors formalize Stored-Noise Deception (SND), introduce Counterfactual Composition Testing for detection, and propose Memory-Persistent Information-Flow Control for mitigation.
result: SND attacks achieve full effect within five sessions, evade four safety classifiers, and persist indefinitely; Counterfactual Composition Testing achieves 87.5% accuracy with zero false positives.
conclusion: The work highlights a critical vulnerability in agentic AI systems and provides effective defenses, but the findings are specific to AI security and not directly applicable to the user's research interests.

title: Beyond Zero: Enterprise Security For The Ai Era
authors: Michal Zalewski Joseph Valente
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of autonomous AI agents and the accelerating velocity of corporate data access are stretching the application-centric model of zero trust security to its breaking point. This paper introduces Beyond Zero, a new security paradigm designed for the AI era. The Beyond Zero architecture performs per-resource and method access decisions for humans and agents at machine speed. By shrinking the trust boundary from the application level to the individual action, and by coupling static authorization guarantees with dynamic, AI-driven reasoning, Beyond Zero enables a self-defending enterprise capable of mediating thousands of human and machine decisions per second. This paper outlines Google's vision for the future of this access model as well a call for industry collaboration and standards development.
tldr: This paper proposes a new enterprise security paradigm called Beyond Zero for the AI era, focusing on per-resource access decisions and AI-driven reasoning.
motivation: The rise of autonomous AI agents and high-velocity data access is breaking traditional zero trust security models.
method: The paper outlines an architecture that shrinks trust boundaries to individual actions and combines static authorization with dynamic AI reasoning.
result: The proposed model enables self-defending enterprises capable of mediating thousands of decisions per second.
conclusion: The paper presents Google's vision and calls for industry collaboration and standards development.

title: Botnet Detection On Ctu-13 Using Lightweight Machine Learning Models
authors: Subhash Gurappa, Yashas Hariprasad, Sundararaj Sitharama Iyengar, Naveen Kumar Chaudhary
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Botnets are among the most persistent cyber threats, enabling large-scale attacks such as spam, credential theft, and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS). While deep learning approaches have recently been applied to botnet detection, they are computationally intensive and often lack interpretability. We present a comparative study of lightweight machine learning models including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest on the CTU-13 dataset, a benchmark for botnet traffic analysis. We extract interpretable flow-based features and evaluate each model on detection accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and feature importance. Results demonstrate that lightweight models can achieve competitive detection performance with minimal computational cost, while also offering interpretability critical for forensic investigation. On CTU-13, our Random Forest achieves a PR-AUC of approximately 0.54 and ROC-AUC of 0.97 while training over 90% faster than published CNN baselines. These results demonstrate that lightweight models can match or exceed deep-learning performance under natural class imbalance while maintaining interpretability and low computational cost.
tldr: This paper compares lightweight machine learning models for botnet detection on the CTU-13 dataset, achieving competitive performance with low computational cost.
motivation: Botnets are a major cyber threat, and deep learning methods are computationally intensive and lack interpretability, motivating the need for lightweight alternatives.
method: The authors evaluate Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest on the CTU-13 dataset using interpretable flow-based features, measuring accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and feature importance.
result: Random Forest achieved a PR-AUC of 0.54 and ROC-AUC of 0.97, training over 90% faster than CNN baselines, demonstrating competitive performance with minimal computational cost.
conclusion: Lightweight models can match or exceed deep learning performance for botnet detection while offering interpretability and low computational overhead, making them suitable for forensic investigation.

title: Complete First-order Reasoning For Functional Programs
authors: Adithya Murali, Lucas Pe\~na, Ranjit Jhala, P. Madhusudan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several practical tools for automatically verifying functional programs (e.g., Liquid Haskell and Leon for Scala programs) rely on a heuristic based on unrolling recursive function definitions followed by quantifier-free reasoning using SMT solvers. We uncover foundational theoretical properties of this heuristic, revealing that it can be generalized and formalized as a technique that is in fact complete for reasoning with combined First-Order theories of algebraic datatypes and background theories, where background theories support decidable quantifier-free reasoning. The theory developed in this paper explains the efficacy of these heuristics when they succeed, explains why they fail when they fail, and the precise role that user help plays in making proofs succeed.
tldr: This paper proves completeness of a heuristic for first-order reasoning over functional programs with algebraic datatypes and background theories.
motivation: To understand why existing verification tools like Liquid Haskell succeed or fail, and to formalize their heuristic approach.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework that generalizes the unrolling heuristic and prove its completeness for combined first-order theories of algebraic datatypes and decidable quantifier-free background theories.
result: The heuristic is complete for such theories, explaining its efficacy and pinpointing where user help is needed.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational theory for automated verification of functional programs, guiding tool improvements and user interaction.

title: PoisonForge: Task-Level Targeted Poisoning Benchmark For Instruction-Tuned LLMs
authors: Luze Sun, Anshuman Suri, Harsh Chaudhari, Cristina Nita-Rotaru, Alina Oprea
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When practitioners fine-tune LLMs on unvetted datasets, an adversary can exploit the data supply chain through task-level poisoning: inserting a small number of crafted instruction-response pairs that cause the model to embed attacker-specified entities, such as a country, in outputs for a targeted task family while behaving normally elsewhere. We introduce PoisonForge, a benchmark that parameterizes this threat along four dimensions (bias type, poisoning mode, appearance count, and target output length) and evaluates 12 open-weight models (from 2B to 32B parameters) across five families under a primarily 1% poison budget. With only 10 poisoned examples among 1,000 fine-tuning examples, 11 of 12 models exceed a 70% attack success rate (ASR) in their most vulnerable configuration. Meanwhile, unintended leakage to non-target tasks remains below 0.5%, and models perform well on standard benchmarks. We analyze in detail the factors contributing to attack success. We observe that multiple appearances of an entity increase the ASR, the optimal poisoning mode depends on the semantic structure of the target entity, and ASR drops monotonically with the task output length. A correlation analysis and risk prediction model confirm that poisoning design choices, rather than model scale, are the primary causes of attack success, and that these patterns generalize to predict attack success on new tasks. We release all configurations, pipelines, and analysis code to support reproducible comparisons.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark for task-level targeted poisoning attacks on instruction-tuned LLMs, showing high attack success with minimal poisoned data.
motivation: To systematically study and parameterize the threat of task-level poisoning in LLM fine-tuning, where adversaries insert crafted instruction-response pairs to bias model outputs for specific tasks.
method: The authors design PoisonForge, a benchmark varying bias type, poisoning mode, appearance count, and target output length, and evaluate 12 open-weight LLMs (2B-32B parameters) across five model families with a 1% poison budget.
result: With only 10 poisoned examples among 1000, 11 of 12 models exceed 70% attack success rate in their most vulnerable configuration, while unintended leakage to non-target tasks remains below 0.5% and standard benchmark performance is maintained.
conclusion: Poisoning design choices (e.g., appearance count, poisoning mode) are the primary drivers of attack success, not model scale, and the patterns generalize to predict attack success on new tasks.

title: Security, Privacy, And Ethical Risks In OpenClaw
authors: Yutong Jin, Zelin Zhang, Zhijin Lyu, Jianbing Ni
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper systematically investigates the security, privacy, and ethical risks, as well as the traceability challenges of OpenClaw, a locally executable AI agent system for natural language interaction and real-world task completion. While OpenClaw shows strong potential for personal assistance, office automation, cross-platform task management, and information integration, it also raises serious security, privacy, and ethical concerns. By analyzing its system architecture, core functionalities, deployment model, and representative application scenarios, this paper aims to reveal the risks that may arise when such a highly privileged agent is integrated into personal and organizational digital environments. We focus in particular on the challenges associated with persistent local storage, tool invocation, cross-context information aggregation, multi-user interaction, and the integration of plugins and external services. We argue that these issues constitute major barriers to the trustworthy deployment and widespread adoption of this technology. Finally, we summarize the open challenges in security defenses, privacy protection, ethical governance, and traceability in agent use, and call for joint efforts from researchers, developers, deployers, and regulators to build AI agent systems that are safer, more reliable, and more trustworthy.
tldr: This paper analyzes security, privacy, and ethical risks of the OpenClaw AI agent system, but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.
motivation: To systematically investigate risks in locally executable AI agents like OpenClaw, which have high privileges and access to personal data.
method: Analysis of OpenClaw's system architecture, core functionalities, deployment model, and application scenarios to identify risks.
result: Identified risks from persistent local storage, tool invocation, cross-context aggregation, multi-user interaction, and plugin integration.
conclusion: These risks are major barriers to trustworthy deployment; calls for joint efforts in security, privacy, ethics, and traceability.

title: Probabilistically Checkable Proofs For The Existential Theory Of The Reals
authors: Jack Stade
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a PCP theorem for the existential theory of the reals, showing that MAX-ETR-INV is [MATH]-hard to approximate to within some constant factor. The existential theory of the reals (ETR) is a decision problem asking if there exists a set of real-valued variables satisfying some constraints involving polynomials and inequalities, and [MATH] is the complexity class of problems polynomial-time reducible to ETR. Many important geometric problems are known to be [MATH]-complete. [MATH]-hardness results frequently work by a reduction from the [MATH]-complete problem ETR-INV, which asks if there is a an assignment of real variables each in the interval [MATH] satisfying some constraints of form [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH]. MAX-ETR-INV is a related optimization problem that asks, given a set of constraints of form [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], for a feasible (that is, satisfiable with variables in [MATH]) subset of those constraints of the largest possible size. We show that there is some constant [MATH] such that it is [MATH]-hard to approximate MAX-ETR-INV better than a [MATH] factor. This means that even a non-deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can't approximate MAX-ETR-INV better than this factor unless [MATH]. We also give a polynomial-time [MATH]-factor approximation algorithm and a non-deterministic-polynomial-time [MATH]-factor approximation algorithm for MAX-ETR-INV.
tldr: This paper proves a PCP theorem for the existential theory of the reals, showing hardness of approximation for MAX-ETR-INV.
motivation: To establish computational hardness results for geometric optimization problems that are complete for the complexity class ∃R.
method: The authors develop a probabilistically checkable proof (PCP) system for ETR and use it to prove that approximating MAX-ETR-INV is ∃R-hard.
result: MAX-ETR-INV is ∃R-hard to approximate within some constant factor, and polynomial-time and nondeterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithms are given.
conclusion: This work extends PCP theory to the existential theory of the reals, with implications for the approximability of geometric problems.

title: When Youth Enter The Algorithmic Wild: Discovering And Understanding Potentially Harmful Teen Videos On Douyin And Kwai
authors: Shaoxuan Zhou, Yafei Sun, Jing Zhang, Xianghang Mi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-video platforms like Douyin and Kwai have become central to adolescent digital life, but they also risk exposing teens to algorithmically amplified harmful content. Despite its societal importance, the scale, mechanisms, and real-world impact of this exposure remain poorly understood. Measuring it is challenging: recommendation feeds are personalized black boxes, harmful content employs sophisticated evasion tactics, and naive crawlers fail to replicate authentic teen behavior. To bridge this gap, we propose PHTV-Scout, the first large-scale, behaviorally grounded measurement framework for Potentially Harmful Teen Videos (PHTVs). We integrate an offline survey of 683 adolescents with a tri-module online pipeline: (1) PHTV Hunter simulates teen accounts to collect recommendation feeds; (2) PHTV Arbiter, a LoRA-finetuned multimodal classifier, detects PHTVs with 94.29% accuracy and 96.41% precision; and (3) PHTV Analyzer performs fine-grained categorization and impact assessment. Over six months, we analyzed 186,727 videos and 51,287 comments, uncovering a troubling 6.11% PHTV prevalence--dominated by Child Sexual Exploitation Imagery (53.2%)--and revealing that harmful content thrives through covert interactions (e.g., grooming comments, self-disclosure) and active evasion (semantic camouflage, noise injection). Crucially, while Youth Mode blocks 100% of PHTVs, its low adoption (30-41%) leaves most teens unprotected. We further show that exposure is driven not by user identity but by regulation, platform algorithms, and even passive browsing, exposing the fragility of adolescent information environments. Our findings call for a paradigm shift from reactive takedowns to proactive, human-centered safeguards.
tldr: This paper studies harmful teen videos on short-video platforms, with no connection to quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or machine learning.
motivation: To understand the prevalence and mechanisms of harmful content exposure to teens on Douyin and Kwai.
method: Combined offline survey with online pipeline including simulated teen accounts, a fine-tuned multimodal classifier, and analysis of videos and comments.
result: Found 6.11% PHTV prevalence, dominated by Child Sexual Exploitation Imagery, and that harmful content uses evasion tactics; Youth Mode blocks all PHTVs but adoption is low.
conclusion: Calls for proactive, human-centered safeguards rather than reactive takedowns.

title: Adversarial Vulnerability Under Temporal Concept Drift: A Longitudinal Study Of Android Malware Detection
authors: Ahmed Sabbah, Mohammed Kharma, Radi Jarrar, Samer Zein, David Mohaisen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a longitudinal, drift-aware evaluation of adversarial robustness across more than a decade of Android applications using static and dynamic feature representations extracted from emulator and real-device executions. The dataset is organized into yearly slices and evaluated under three deployment protocols that emulate realistic learning scenarios: (1) same-year training and testing, (2) cross-year deployment without model updates, and (3) expanding-window retraining with cumulative historical data. Across multiple classifier families, adversarial examples are generated using FGSM and SPSA under feasibility constraints. We measure clean performance, Adversarial Accuracy (AA), Attack Success Rate (ASR), and introduce temporal linkage metrics -- RobustDrop, [MATH]ASR, and Adversarial Amplification Factor (AAF) -- to quantify the relationship between distribution shift and robustness degradation.nResults show that temporal separation is associated with reduced adversarial robustness under the evaluated transfer-based feature-space setting. As the train-test gap increases, clean accuracy and adversarial accuracy decline, while attack success exhibits configuration-dependent increases, particularly under FGSM perturbations and static features. Expanding-window retraining mitigates, but does not eliminate, robustness loss under continued distributional evolution. These findings indicate that temporal drift should be considered when assessing the long-term robustness of intelligent detection systems under evolving data distributions and highlight the need for drift-aware robustness assessment frameworks in long-lived adversarial environments.
tldr: This paper studies adversarial robustness of Android malware detection under temporal concept drift, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To evaluate how adversarial robustness of malware detectors degrades over time due to distribution shifts in Android apps.
method: Longitudinal study using static/dynamic features from emulator/real-device executions, yearly slices, three deployment protocols, and FGSM/SPSA adversarial attacks.
result: Temporal separation reduces adversarial robustness; expanding-window retraining mitigates but does not eliminate robustness loss.
conclusion: Temporal drift should be considered in long-term robustness assessment of intelligent detection systems.

title: Less Effort, Shorter Proofs: Reinforcement Learning For Security Protocol Analysis In Tamarin
authors: Matthias Cosler, Cas Cremers, Bernd Finkbeiner, Mohamed Ghanem, Niklas Medinger
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tools like Tamarin and ProVerif have achieved notable success in analyzing and verifying complex real-world protocols such as EMV, 5G, and WPA2, even detecting zero-day exploits. Despite these successes, verifying such protocols remains a time-consuming, challenging task, often requiring significant human effort and expertise. In this paper, we present a reinforcement learning (RL) framework inspired by AlphaZero and AlphaProof that implements a new style of proof search for Tamarin. We have developed a stateless API for Tamarin that acts as a classical RL environment. We guide a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) by a neural heuristic that learns from completed subproofs. We evaluate our framework on 16 case studies, ranging from classical protocol models to challenging state-of-the-art protocol models from recent publications. Our method finds more proofs automatically than Tamarin's standard search and produces shorter proofs than both the standard and human-engineered heuristics. Our pipeline is applicable out of the box to assist Tamarin users in active research, reducing the human effort required. Moreover, our standardized interface provides a programmatic way for users to interact with Tamarin. Finally, our work demonstrates the promising potential of adapting RL-based methods to the Tamarin domain.
tldr: This paper applies reinforcement learning to improve proof search in the Tamarin security protocol analyzer, reducing human effort and producing shorter proofs.
motivation: Verifying complex security protocols like EMV, 5G, and WPA2 is time-consuming and requires significant human expertise; the authors aim to automate and shorten the proof search process.
method: The authors develop a stateless API for Tamarin that acts as a reinforcement learning environment, using Monte Carlo Tree Search guided by a neural heuristic trained on completed subproofs, inspired by AlphaZero and AlphaProof.
result: The RL-based method finds more proofs automatically than Tamarin's standard search and produces shorter proofs than both standard and human-engineered heuristics across 16 case studies.
conclusion: The approach reduces human effort in protocol verification and demonstrates the potential of RL-based methods in the Tamarin domain, with an out-of-the-box pipeline for active research.

title: Super Condorcet Winners And Limit Coalitional Manipulability Of Irv
authors: Fran\c{c}ois Durand (UPC), \'elie de Panafieu (UPC), Guillem Perarnau
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the limit CM rate of single-winner voting rules under Impartial Culture, defined as the probability that a preference profile is coalitionally manipulable in the limit of large electorates. For m = 3 candidates, Lepelley and Valognes [1999] derived a closed-form expression for Plurality with Runoff, or equivalently Instant-Runoff Voting (IRV), and showed that its limit CM rate is strictly below 1. This is remarkable because Kim and Roush [1996] established a limit of 1 for several major rules, including Maximin and all positional scoring rules except Veto. In this paper, we generalize the result of Lepelley and Valognes to any number of candidates m [MATH] 4. We show that Plurality with Runoff has a limit CM rate equal to 1 for all m [MATH] 4, whereas IRV retains a limit CM rate strictly below 1. To this end, we rely on the notion of Super Condorcet Winner, recently introduced by Durand [2025], which yields an upper bound on the CM rate of IRV. We prove that this bound is asymptotically tight and compute the probability that a Super Condorcet Winner exists, thereby obtaining the exact limit CM rate of IRV.
tldr: This paper studies the limit coalitional manipulability of Instant-Runoff Voting and Plurality with Runoff for any number of candidates, showing that IRV retains a manipulability rate strictly below 1 while Plurality with Runoff becomes fully manipulable for four or more candidates.
motivation: To understand the asymptotic vulnerability of single-winner voting rules to coalitional manipulation, extending previous results for three candidates to any number of candidates.
method: The authors use the concept of Super Condorcet Winner to derive an upper bound on the coalitional manipulability rate of IRV, and prove this bound is asymptotically tight by computing the probability that a Super Condorcet Winner exists under Impartial Culture.
result: For m ≥ 4 candidates, Plurality with Runoff has a limit CM rate of 1 (fully manipulable), while IRV has a limit CM rate strictly below 1, given by the probability that a Super Condorcet Winner exists.
conclusion: IRV is asymptotically less manipulable than Plurality with Runoff for more than three candidates, providing theoretical justification for IRV's resistance to coalitional manipulation in large electorates.

title: Routing Equilibrium In Mixed-Autonomy Traffic Networks With Altruistic Autonomous Agents
authors: Ermin Wei Lihui Yi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.23782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advancements in vehicle autonomy have drawn interest in understanding the impact of autonomous vehicles on traffic systems. In this paper, we study a traffic assignment problem in a mixed-autonomy setting where both human-driven and autonomous vehicles coexist. We model the interaction as a simultaneous routing game where human drivers are self-interested and aim to minimize their own travel times, while autonomous agents are altruistic and aim to minimize the total social cost. The standard nonatomic congestion game analysis establishes the existence of equilibrium to this game under convex cost functions, and does not have any implication of its uniqueness. In this work, we formulate the equilibrium as a variational inequality (VI), which enables us to establish the equilibrium existence without convexity assumption, and guarantees the uniqueness of the aggregated link flow and social cost at equilibrium under a specific class of cost functions. Leveraging this VI framework, we provide sufficient conditions under which including autonomous agents improves, deteriorates, or has no effect on social cost. While the possibility of deterioration has been established in prior work, our results complement existing worst-case bounds by explicitly characterizing sufficient conditions under which each outcome occurs, thereby providing a deeper understanding of mixed-autonomy traffic systems. Furthermore, we consider a centralized scenario where a social planner optimizes the routing of autonomous agents, and show that the same equilibrium is achieved as in the decentralized scenario when assuming convex costs.Finally, we conduct numerical experiments that illustrate how social cost changes with the amount of autonomous vehicles under different system parameters.
tldr: This paper studies routing equilibrium in mixed-autonomy traffic networks with altruistic autonomous agents, using variational inequality and game theory.
motivation: To understand the impact of autonomous vehicles on traffic systems and provide conditions under which social cost improves or deteriorates.
method: Formulates the routing game as a variational inequality, establishes existence and uniqueness of equilibrium, and compares decentralized and centralized scenarios.
result: Provides sufficient conditions for social cost improvement, deterioration, or no effect; shows equivalence of decentralized and centralized equilibria under convex costs.
conclusion: Offers deeper understanding of mixed-autonomy traffic systems and conditions for beneficial deployment of autonomous vehicles.
